vrf.title: VRF (separate routing tables)
vrf.intro: A VRF is a separate routing table on the same device. Ports in a VRF only see its networks and routes, so two customers can use the same addresses. Routing protocols, NAT and automatic routing only apply to the global table.
vrf.delete: Delete VRF {name} (ports return to the global table)
vrf.empty: no networks yet: assign a port and set an address
vxlan.title: VXLAN (VLAN across the routed network)
vxlan.intro: As a VTEP the switch wraps frames of a VLAN in UDP (VXLAN) and sends them to the other VTEPs of the same VNI. Devices at different sites are thus in the same layer-2 network, with routing in between.
vxlan.hint: Usual: a loopback as source, reachable in the underlay via OSPF. Command line: «vlan 10», «vn-segment 10010», «interface nve1», «source-interface loopback0», «member vni 10010 peer-ip 10.255.0.2», «show nve vni», «show nve peers». EVPN (BGP as control plane) is not modelled: the VTEPs are a fixed list.
feature.net.vxlan.hint: Extend VLANs across routed networks (layer-3 switch as VTEP)
vrf.hint: Command line: «vrf definition CUSTOMER-A», on the interface «vrf forwarding CUSTOMER-A», «ip route vrf CUSTOMER-A 0.0.0.0/0 10.1.1.2», «show ip route vrf CUSTOMER-A», «ping vrf CUSTOMER-A 10.1.1.2».
feature.net.vrf.hint: Several routing tables on one router (e.g. two customers)

error.invalidIp: “{value}” is not a valid IPv4 address. Expected four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, e.g. 192.168.0.10.
error.invalidIp6: “{value}” is not a valid IPv6 address for a port. Expected e.g. 2001:db8:1::10/64 (eight blocks of four hex digits, “::” shortens zeros). Link-local and multicast addresses are not allowed.
error.ipv6Link: With a link-local address (fe80::…) as next router, the port must be given: it is only valid on one link.
error.invalidMask: “{value}” is not a valid subnet mask. The ones must be contiguous from the left, e.g. 255.255.255.0 or /24.
error.maskRequired: An IP address needs a subnet mask. It defines which part of the address identifies the network.
error.gatewayWithoutAddress: A default gateway only works if the device itself has an IP address.
warning.reservedAddress: {ip} is reserved (0.x, 127.x for loopback, or 224.x and above for multicast) and is not suitable for a device.

warning.broadcastAddress: {ip} is the broadcast address of {net}. Packets to this address go to all devices in the network.

warning.gatewayIsSelf: The device is entered as its own default gateway.

adapter.title: Adapter
adapter.macHint: Formats like 02-00-00-AA-BB-CC or 0200.00aa.bbcc. Enter saves, Esc cancels.
adapter.duplicateMac: This MAC address exists twice in the same network. The switch learns it alternately on two ports; packets reach the wrong device and connections drop.
subnet.summary: Network {net}: host addresses {first} to {last} ({hosts} in total), broadcast {broadcast}
subnet.pointToPoint: Network {net}: point-to-point link with {hosts} address(es), without network and broadcast address
actions.arpEmpty: No entries yet. They appear as soon as the device communicates with others.
switch.explain: The switch remembers which MAC address is behind which port. Frames to known addresses only go to that port; broadcasts and unknown addresses go to all ports.
switch.macEmpty: Still empty. The switch learns from the source addresses of the frames it receives.
modem.explain: The modem passes frames unchanged between its two ports (simplified WAN link).
router.noRoutes: None. The router knows directly connected networks by itself.
firewall.title: Firewall rules
acl.title: Access lists (ACL)
acl.intro: An ACL checks IP packets arriving on a port: rules from top to bottom, the first match wins, an implicit «deny» comes last. Stateless: replies also need a matching rule on the port they arrive on.
acl.unused: not applied to a port (has no effect)
acl.svisHint: “in” checks everything coming from the VLAN (also to the switch itself, e.g. DHCP to the relay). “out” checks what is routed into the VLAN. A ping needs both directions (echo request and reply).
acl.hint: ARP, spanning tree and IPv6 neighbour discovery always pass. Command line: «ip access-list extended NAME», «permit tcp any host 192.168.10.80 eq 80», on the port «ip access-group NAME in», «show access-lists».
firewall.scopeRouter: The firewall checks packets the router forwards. The first matching rule decides, otherwise the default rule applies.
firewall.scopeDevice: The firewall checks packets it forwards and packets addressed to itself. The first matching rule decides, otherwise the default rule applies. Zones: eth0 WAN, eth1 LAN, eth2 DMZ, further ports OPT.
firewall.scopeHost: The firewall checks packets arriving at this device. What the device sends itself is always allowed.
firewall.hitsHint: How often the rule matched in this simulation
firewall.stateful: Stateful: replies to allowed connections come back automatically
firewall.hint: Source and destination: «any», an address (192.168.2.80) or a network (192.168.1.0/24). Order matters: put specific rules at the top.
vpn.title: VPN tunnels (IPsec)
vpn.intro: A site-to-site VPN connects the local network to the network of another site, encrypted. The other router needs the mirrored tunnel with the same key.
vpn.name: Name
vpn.hint: The tunnel is set up with the first packet to the remote network (IKEv2). After that packets travel wrapped in ESP: outside the router addresses, inside the encrypted original. NAT does not apply to tunnel traffic.
router.routeUnusable: Not usable: the gateway is not in any connected network.
routing.title: Routing table
routing.empty: Empty. Give the interfaces IP addresses first.
routing.addHint: Enter a new static route in the last row: destination network, mask, next hop (or just the interface), then add it with +.
canvas.duplicateIp: Address assigned twice: {ip}. Two devices in the same network must not share an IP address.
canvas.duplicateMac: Duplicate MAC address in the same network: {mac}. The switch no longer knows which port the device is on.
demo.title: Demo networks
demo.intro: A ready-made network for every protocol. «Present» starts the simulation and triggers the matching action so the class can watch. «Open» loads the network into design mode to explore. Undo brings back your current project.
demo.arpPing.title: ARP and ping in the LAN
demo.arpPing.text: Three computers on a switch, all in 192.168.1.0/24.
demo.arpPing.show: PC 1 asks for PC 2's MAC with an ARP broadcast, then four ICMP echoes follow. The switch learns its MAC table.
demo.gateway.title: Default gateway
demo.gateway.text: Two subnets connected by a router.
demo.gateway.show: PC 1 sees that the target is in another network and sends the packet to its router. The TTL drops by one.
demo.dhcp.title: DHCP (DORA)
demo.dhcp.text: A server assigns addresses to three clients.
demo.dhcp.show: Discover, offer, request, ack for each client; then «ipconfig /all» shows the leased address.
demo.web.title: DNS, TCP and HTTP
demo.dns.title: DNS with forwarding
demo.dns.text: School DNS with the zone schule.example (A, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, PTR) that forwards unknown names to the provider's DNS.
demo.dns.show: PC 1 resolves an alias through two CNAMEs, looks up the mail server (MX) and opens a page at the provider: the school DNS forwards the question and answers “non-authoritative”.
demo.dns.tour.0: The school DNS holds the zone schule.example: A records for addresses, CNAME for aliases, MX for the mail server, TXT for text (here an SPF rule), NS for the name server and PTR for reverse lookup. Below is the forwarding to the provider.
demo.dns.tour.1: PC 1 asks for intranet.schule.example. That is an alias for www, and www is an alias for web. The server follows the chain and returns everything in one answer. Look at PC 1's console.
demo.dns.tour.2: Now the domain's mail server: “nslookup -type=MX schule.example”. With several MX records, the smallest preference wins.
demo.dns.tour.3: And backwards: “nslookup 192.168.10.3” asks for the PTR record 3.10.168.192.in-addr.arpa and gets the web server's name.
demo.dns.tour.4: www.provider.example is not in the school zone. The school DNS forwards the question to the provider DNS, caches the answer and passes it to PC 1 as “non-authoritative”. Then the browser loads the page.
demo.dns.tour.5: The school DNS console shows every query: from the zone, forwarded or from the cache. Try it yourself: nslookup -type=TXT schule.example or a name that does not exist.
demo.ipv6Services.title: Web, mail and SSH over IPv6
demo.ipv6Services.text: A pure IPv6 network: the PC gets its address and DNS server from the router (SLAAC and RDNSS), the school DNS has AAAA records, the web and mail server sits in the second network.
demo.ipv6Services.show: PC 1 resolves www.schule.example via AAAA, loads the page over TCP and IPv6 and sends a mail by SMTP. The filter “ipv6 and tcp” shows the application traffic.
demo.ipv6Services.tour.0: The router has two IPv6 networks. The left port also lists a DNS server: the router sends it along in the router advertisement (RDNSS option).
demo.ipv6Services.tour.1: The school DNS holds AAAA records: they map a name to an IPv6 address, like A records do for IPv4. Plus an MX for mail and a PTR under ip6.arpa.
demo.ipv6Services.tour.2: PC 1 is set to “IPv6 automatic”. From the router advertisement it forms its address (SLAAC) and takes over the DNS server. Look at its state.
demo.ipv6Services.tour.3: “nslookup www.schule.example” asks the DNS server over IPv6 for the AAAA record.
demo.ipv6Services.tour.4: The browser resolves the name and opens a TCP connection to [2001:db8:b::80]:80. The handshake and the HTTP request work exactly as with IPv4, just inside an IPv6 packet (next header 6 = TCP).
demo.ipv6Services.tour.5: Now a mail to ben@schule.example: SMTP over IPv6 to the server mail.schule.example, which DNS knows via AAAA.
demo.ipv6Services.tour.6: Try it yourself: “ssh admin@router.schule.example” (password Netz2026), “ping www.schule.example”, “nslookup 2001:db8:b::80” or “netstat”.
demo.web.text: A notebook fetches a web page through a router.
demo.web.show: DNS query for www.schule.example, TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and the HTTP request in the browser.
demo.mail.title: Email: SMTP, POP3, IMAP
demo.mail.text: Anna and Ben share a mail server.
demo.mail.show: Anna sends via SMTP, Ben fetches the message via IMAP.
demo.vlanStp.title: VLAN and spanning tree
demo.vlanStp.text: Three switches in a ring, two VLANs over trunks.
demo.vlanStp.show: STP blocks one port (orange), then the office reaches its second computer over the trunk with an 802.1Q tag.
demo.storm.title: Broadcast storm
demo.storm.text: Three switches in a ring, but without spanning tree.
demo.storm.show: The very first ARP request circles endlessly and multiplies. Then enable STP and compare.
demo.duplicateMac.title: Duplicate MAC address
demo.duplicateMac.text: Three computers on a switch; the notebook has the same MAC address as PC 2.
demo.duplicateMac.show: PC 1 pings PC 2 while the notebook pings PC 1. The switch learns the MAC alternately on two ports and reports «MAC moves»; replies reach the wrong device and pings are lost.
demo.duplicateMac.tour.0: Three computers are connected to a switch. Look at the notebook's ports: its MAC address is the same as PC 2's. That is why both show a red exclamation mark.
demo.duplicateMac.tour.1: I start the simulation and PC 1 pings PC 2. So far everything is normal: the switch learns which port PC 2 is on.
demo.duplicateMac.tour.2: Now the notebook sends too – with the same source MAC. The switch thinks PC 2 has moved and sends its frames to the notebook from now on.
demo.duplicateMac.tour.3: The switch's state shows the MAC table, and its console reports «MAC moves from port … to port …». Real switches log this as «MAC flapping».
demo.duplicateMac.tour.4: PC 1 loses pings or gets replies only some of the time. Fix: give every device its own MAC address (reset it to «Factory» in the ports window).
demo.routerOnAStick.title: Router on a stick
demo.routerOnAStick.text: Two VLANs, one router with subinterfaces on the trunk.
demo.routerOnAStick.show: The packet goes tagged to the router (eth0.10) and comes out in the other VLAN (eth0.20).
demo.l3switch.title: Layer 3 switch and DHCP relay
demo.l3switch.text: A core switch routes between three VLANs, the DHCP server is central.
demo.l3switch.show: The SVIs relay DHCP; then notebook 1 pings the server across the VLAN boundary.
demo.l3switchIpv6.title: IPv6 on the layer 3 switch
demo.l3switchIpv6.text: The core switch has an IPv6 address per VLAN (SVI) and routes between the VLANs. Floor 1 gets addresses by SLAAC, floor 2 by DHCPv6.
demo.l3switchIpv6.show: The SVIs send router advertisements over the trunks into their VLAN. Notebook 2 pings notebook 1 across the VLAN boundary, then notebook 1 opens the intranet by name (AAAA).
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.0: On the core switch every VLAN interface has an IPv6 address. VLAN 20 hands out addresses by DHCPv6, all VLANs name the server as DNS server (RDNSS).
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.1: Notebook 1 in VLAN 10 forms its address from the prefix 2001:db8:10::/64 and its MAC (SLAAC). The default gateway is the link-local address of the SVI.
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.2: Notebook 2 in VLAN 20 sees the M flag in the router advertisement and gets its address by DHCPv6 from the switch.
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.3: Ping across the VLAN boundary: the frame arrives tagged over the trunk at the core, the VLAN 20 SVI accepts it and the switch routes it into VLAN 10.
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.4: Notebook 1 opens http://intranet.schule.example/: DNS over IPv6 returns the AAAA record, then HTTP over TCP and IPv6 into the server VLAN.
demo.l3switchIpv6.tour.5: The core switch state lists the IPv6 neighbours per VLAN interface. Try “show ipv6 interface brief” and “show ipv6 route” on the switch command line.
demo.static.title: Static routes
demo.static.text: Two routers, each knows the remote network through a static route.
demo.static.show: «tracert» shows both routers as hops. Delete a route and try again: destination network unreachable.
demo.autoRouting.title: Automatic routing
demo.autoRouting.text: Three routers, three networks and not a single route entered: automatic routing finds the paths by itself.
demo.autoRouting.show: «tracert» from PC A to PC C shows every router on the way. Untick one router: the destination can no longer be reached.
demo.autoRouting.tour.0: Three routers connect three networks. Nobody has entered any routes. Even so, all PCs should reach each other.
demo.autoRouting.tour.1: «Automatic routing» is ticked on every router. The preview shows the calculated routes marked «A», e.g. 192.168.30.0/24 via Router 2.
demo.autoRouting.tour.2: PC A traces the path to PC C with «tracert». Each router looks in its table and sends the packet on to the next router.
demo.autoRouting.tour.3: Router 2 knows every network: on the left via Router 1, on the right via Router 3, PC B is directly connected. The metric counts the routers to the destination.
demo.autoRouting.tour.4: Try it yourself: in design mode, untick Router 1. It then only knows its own networks, and PC C can no longer be reached. The «Static routes» and «OSPF» demos show how to solve this by hand.
demo.ospf.title: OSPF
demo.ospf.text: Three routers in a triangle learn their networks via OSPF.
demo.ospf.show: Hello, DBD, LSU, LSAck in the packet list; the routing table fills with O routes. Then remove a cable: OSPF recalculates.
demo.ospfv3.title: OSPFv3 for IPv6
demo.ospfv3.text: The same three routers as for OSPF, but IPv6 only: they learn their prefixes by OSPFv3.
demo.ospfv3.show: Hellos to ff02::5 from the link-local addresses, then DBD, LSR, LSU, LSAck. The IPv6 routing table fills with O routes; tracert takes the shortest path.
demo.ospfv3.tour.0: On R1, OSPFv3 takes interfaces, not networks as in OSPFv2. The interface to the PC is passive: its prefix is announced, but no hellos are sent there.
demo.ospfv3.tour.1: The routers send hellos to ff02::5, with their link-local address as source. Filter the packet list with “ospfv3”.
demo.ospfv3.tour.2: R2’s state lists the neighbours (full) and the database: router LSAs describe the links, intra-area prefix LSAs the networks.
demo.ospfv3.tour.3: PC 1 traces the route to PC 2. The routers forward to the next router’s link-local address, but tracert shows their global addresses.
demo.ospfv3.tour.4: Try it: remove the cable between R1 and R2. OSPFv3 notices after the dead interval and computes a path via R3. On R1’s command line: “show ipv6 ospf6 neighbor”, “show ipv6 route”.
demo.ripng.title: RIPng for IPv6
demo.ripng.text: Three routers learn their IPv6 prefixes by RIPng: distance vector with hop count, like RIP v2.
demo.ripng.show: Updates by UDP 521 to ff02::9. The IPv6 routing table fills with R routes, tracert finds the way to PC 2.
demo.rip.title: RIP
demo.rip.text: The same triangle, this time with RIP v2 (distance vector).
demo.rip.show: Regular updates via UDP 520; the metric counts hops.
demo.bgp.title: BGP between autonomous systems
demo.bgp.show: BGP sessions over TCP 179, OPEN and UPDATE with a growing AS path, then a ping across all three systems.
demo.nat.title: NAT and port forwarding
demo.nat.text: Home network with private addresses behind a NAT router.
demo.nat.show: The PC opens a public web page; the router's NAT table shows the translation to the public address.
demo.snat.title: SNAT: replacing the source address
demo.snat.text: Company network with PAT for everyone and static SNAT for the mail server.
demo.snat.show: PC 1 appears outside as 203.0.113.2 with a different port (PAT), the mail server always as 203.0.113.5 (static SNAT). The router's NAT table shows both types.
demo.dnat.title: DNAT: replacing the destination address
demo.dnat.text: Internal web server under its own public address, plus a port forward to the NAS.
demo.dnat.show: «Outside» opens 203.0.113.5; the router replaces the destination with 192.168.0.80 and the reply leaves with 203.0.113.5 again. Then try http://203.0.113.2:8080/ (port forward).
demo.cpe.title: Internet box (CPE) on cable
demo.cpe.text: Two computers on an internet box with cable modem, NAT and DHCP.
demo.cpe.show: First the box brings up the DOCSIS line, the computers get an address via DHCP, then the notebook loads a web page from the internet.
demo.ppp.title: Serial WAN link with PPP
demo.ppp.text: Zurich and Bern connected by a serial line.
demo.ppp.show: LCP and IPCP negotiate the link, then IP packets flow without MAC addresses.
demo.wlan.title: Wi-Fi with mesh
demo.wlan.text: Two mesh access points over two floors.
demo.wlan.show: The notebook upstairs reaches the server over the wireless mesh. Move the notebook: it switches access points (roaming).
demo.arpPing.tour.0: Hi! I'll show you how a ping works in a local network. Three computers are connected to a switch, all with an address from 192.168.1.0/24.
demo.arpPing.tour.1: PC 1 has 192.168.1.10/24. The target 192.168.1.11 is in the same network. So PC 1 doesn't need a router, but it does need PC 2's MAC address.
demo.arpPing.tour.2: I'm starting the simulation and the ping, but pausing it. Now press «Single step» (key N) and watch the packets travel.
demo.arpPing.tour.3: First PC 1 asks with an ARP broadcast «Who has 192.168.1.11?». The switch sends the broadcast to all ports and remembers which port PC 1 is on.
demo.arpPing.tour.4: PC 2 replies directly to PC 1. Now PC 1 knows the MAC address and sends the ICMP echo. In single step you can see: the switch only unpacks up to layer 2, PC 2 all the way.
demo.arpPing.tour.5: I'm letting the simulation continue. In the switch's window under «State» you see the MAC table it has learned. Well done!
demo.gateway.tour.0: There are two networks here: 192.168.1.0/24 on the left and 192.168.2.0/24 on the right. A router sits in between.
demo.gateway.tour.1: PC 1 has 192.168.1.1 as its default gateway. Everything outside its own network goes there.
demo.gateway.tour.2: The router knows both networks because it has an address in each. You can see that in its routing table: two «C» entries for directly connected.
demo.gateway.tour.3: Now PC 1 pings PC 2. Continue with «Single step»: PC 1 uses ARP to find the router's MAC, not PC 2's! The router unpacks up to layer 3, reads the destination IP and forwards.
demo.gateway.tour.4: PC 2's replies come back with TTL 63: PC 2 starts at 64 and the router lowers the TTL by one. That's how you can tell how many routers are in between.
demo.ipv6.title: IPv6: SLAAC, DHCPv6 and Neighbor Discovery
demo.ipv6.text: A router with two IPv6 networks. On the left the PCs form their own address (SLAAC), on the right the notebook gets one by DHCPv6.
demo.ipv6.show: Router advertisements, duplicate address detection, then a ping with neighbour solicitation instead of ARP. Filter «ndp» shows Neighbor Discovery.
demo.ipv6.tour.0: Welcome to IPv6! IPv4 is switched off entirely here (the top says «IPv6»). None of the three computers has an address entered, all are set to «IPv6 automatic».
demo.ipv6.tour.1: The router has 2001:db8:a::1/64 on the left and 2001:db8:b::1/64 on the right. On the left it only announces the prefix (SLAAC), on the right it asks for DHCPv6 (M flag). Each port also has a link-local address fe80::…
demo.ipv6.tour.2: I start the simulation paused. Use «Single step»: first every device checks with a neighbour solicitation from «::» whether its link-local address is free (DAD). Then the PCs ask for a router with a router solicitation.
demo.ipv6.tour.3: The router answers with a router advertisement to everyone (ff02::1). PC 1 takes the prefix 2001:db8:a:: and appends its interface ID from the MAC (EUI-64). The default gateway is the router's link-local address.
demo.ipv6.tour.4: On the right the router advertisement carries the M flag. So the notebook gets its address by DHCPv6: Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply. It receives 2001:db8:b::100.
demo.ipv6.tour.5: PC 1 pings the notebook. In single step you see: instead of an ARP broadcast, PC 1 asks a multicast group for the router's MAC with a neighbour solicitation. The router answers with a neighbour advertisement.
demo.ipv6.tour.6: The replies come back with hop limit 63: the router took one off, like the TTL in IPv4. «ipconfig» shows all addresses, «netsh interface ipv6 show neighbors» the neighbours. Well done!
demo.dhcp.tour.0: Three clients don't have an address yet. They should get one automatically from the server.
demo.dhcp.tour.1: The server runs the DHCP service. It assigns addresses from a range, along with mask, gateway and DNS server.
demo.dhcp.tour.2: I'm starting the simulation paused. Continue with «Single step»: each client first calls out «DHCP Discover» by broadcast, because it doesn't know the server yet.
demo.dhcp.tour.3: The server answers with an offer. The client requests the address (request) and the server confirms (ack). Remember: DORA.
demo.dhcp.tour.4: Now everything continues. «ipconfig /all» on Notebook 1 shows the leased address, the DHCP server and how long the address is valid.
demo.web.tour.0: The notebook wants to open a web page: http://www.schule.example/. That takes three protocols: DNS, TCP and HTTP.
demo.web.tour.1: This server is the DNS server. It knows the name www.schule.example and its IP address.
demo.web.tour.2: First the notebook gets an address via DHCP. I'm letting the simulation run briefly for that.
demo.web.tour.3: Now the browser opens the page, and I'm pausing. With «Single step»: first the notebook asks the DNS server for the IP address of www.schule.example.
demo.web.tour.4: With the answer, the browser sets up a TCP connection to the web server: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Only then does it send the HTTP request «GET».
demo.web.tour.5: The web server replies with «200 OK» and the page. You see it in the browser, and every single step in the packet list.
demo.snat.tour.0: In the company network everyone has private addresses (192.168.0.x). Private addresses are not allowed on the internet. So the router replaces the source address: SNAT.
demo.snat.tour.1: In the NAT settings you see: port eth1 faces the internet. PAT applies to everyone, and the mail server also has a static SNAT to 203.0.113.5.
demo.snat.tour.2: PC 1 opens a web page. The router replaces 192.168.0.10 with its own address 203.0.113.2 and a free port. That's PAT (masquerading).
demo.snat.tour.3: Now the mail server pings. Outside it always appears as 203.0.113.5, with its port unchanged. That's static SNAT, important e.g. so that other mail servers trust it.
demo.snat.tour.4: The router's NAT table shows both types: PAT with a new port and SNAT with a fixed address. Replies find their way back through these entries.
demo.snat.tour.5: Important: SNAT doesn't let new connections in from outside. That takes DNAT. Have a look at the next demo!
demo.dnat.tour.0: This web server is in the internal network (192.168.0.80). Even so, it should be reachable from the internet.
demo.dnat.tour.1: The router has a static DNAT: requests to 203.0.113.5 go to 192.168.0.80. There's also a port forward: port 8080 of the router address goes to the NAS.
demo.dnat.tour.2: «Outside» opens http://203.0.113.5/. The router replaces the destination address with 192.168.0.80. The web server replies, and the router replaces the source with 203.0.113.5 again.
demo.dnat.tour.3: You can see the DNAT entry in the NAT table. «Outside» never learned that the server actually has a private address.
demo.dnat.tour.4: Now the port forward: http://203.0.113.2:8080/ ends up at the NAS on port 80. That's DNAT too, but only for one port.
demo.dnat.tour.5: In short: SNAT changes the source (inside → outside), DNAT the destination (outside → inside). Try adding another forward yourself in the NAT tab!
demo.cpe.tour.0: This is what an internet connection at home looks like: the provider's internet box (CPE) is modem, router, DHCP server and switch in one.
demo.cpe.tour.1: You only enter the WAN address from the provider and its gateway. In the LAN the box has 192.168.1.1 by factory default and assigns addresses via DHCP.
demo.cpe.tour.2: On start the box first brings up the cable line (DOCSIS): find channel, ranging, registration. Look at the packet list, those are the first frames.
demo.cpe.tour.3: At the same time the PC and notebook get an address from the box via DHCP (192.168.1.100 and .101).
demo.cpe.tour.4: The notebook opens a web page on the internet. The box translates to its WAN address via NAT and sends the packet over the cable line.
demo.cpe.tour.5: In the box's state you see the NAT table and the assigned addresses. That's exactly how the box works at your home!
demo.dsLite.title: DS-Lite: IPv4 in an IPv6 tunnel
demo.dsLite.text: The provider only runs IPv6. The internet box wraps IPv4 in IPv6, the provider's AFTR translates by CGNAT.
demo.dsLite.show: The notebook opens a website that can only be reached over IPv4. Filter «dslite» shows the tunnelled packets.
demo.firewall.title: Firewall with DMZ
demo.firewall.text: A router with a firewall separates LAN, DMZ and Internet. From outside only the web server on port 80 is reachable.
demo.firewall.show: «Aussen» opens the web server (allowed), then pings the office PC (blocked, see the router's console). Filter «tcp.port == 80 or icmp».
demo.firewall.tour.0: The firewall sits between three zones: the LAN with the office PC, the DMZ with the public web server and the Internet («Aussen»).
demo.firewall.tour.1: The rules: 1. HTTP (TCP 80) to the web server is allowed for everyone. 2. Everything may go out from the LAN. The default rule denies everything else. Order matters: the first matching rule wins.
demo.firewall.tour.2: «Aussen» opens http://203.0.113.80/. Rule 1 matches, the page arrives. The web server's replies need no rule of their own: the firewall is stateful and knows the connection.
demo.firewall.tour.3: Now «Aussen» pings the office PC. No rule matches, so the default rule «Deny» applies. The router's console reports every blocked packet.
demo.firewall.tour.4: The other way round works: the office PC pings «Aussen». Rule 2 allows it, and the replies come back thanks to the tracked connection.
demo.firewall.tour.5: The counters show how often each rule matched. Try it yourself: turn off «Stateful» and see what happens to the replies.
demo.firewallZones.title: Firewall device and ACL
demo.portChannel.title: Port-channel with LACP
demo.portChannel.text: Two cables between two switches are bundled into one link with LACP: double bandwidth, redundancy, no loop.
demo.portChannel.show: Filter «lacp»: both switches exchange LACPDUs every second. Then the office PC pings the lab PC through the channel. Spanning tree blocks neither of the two ports.
demo.portChannel.tour.0: There are two cables between the two switches. Without bundling this would be a loop: spanning tree would block one cable, without STP there would be a broadcast storm.
demo.portChannel.tour.1: Both ports are assigned to port-channel 1, mode «LACP active». The other side is set up the same way.
demo.portChannel.tour.2: In the simulation the switches send each other LACPDUs: «I am system X, channel 1, port 2.» Only when both sides know each other are the ports bundled. The console reports «bundled».
demo.portChannel.tour.3: The ping runs through the channel. Each conversation takes one of the cables depending on the MAC addresses; if one fails, everything continues over the other.
demo.portChannel.tour.4: Try «show etherchannel summary» on the command line. If you set one side to «passive» and the other as well, nothing bundles any more: one has to be active.
demo.vxlan.title: VXLAN between two sites
demo.vxlan.text: Two layer-3 switches extend VLAN 10 via VXLAN across a routed network (OSPF). The PCs in Zürich and Bern are in the same subnet.
demo.vxlan.show: First the switches learn the loopbacks (10.255.0.1 and .2) via OSPF. Then the Zürich PC pings the Bern PC: ARP and ping run wrapped in UDP 4789 across the spine. Filter «vxlan».
demo.vxlan.tour.0: Between Zürich and Bern there is a routed network: the spine router only knows transfer networks and loopbacks. A VLAN normally cannot reach across a router.
demo.vxlan.tour.1: The leaf switches are VTEPs: VLAN 10 belongs to VNI 10010, the source is loopback 0, the other VTEP is in the list. OSPF distributes the loopbacks.
demo.vxlan.tour.2: In the simulation the switches first build their OSPF adjacencies. Only once the loopbacks are reachable can the tunnel carry frames.
demo.vxlan.tour.3: The Zürich PC pings the Bern PC in the same subnet. Its ARP request is a broadcast in VLAN 10: the leaf wraps it in VXLAN and sends it by IP to the other VTEP, which unwraps it.
demo.vxlan.tour.4: In the packet list you see outer IPv4 from loopback to loopback, UDP 4789 with VNI 10010, inside the Ethernet frame with ARP or ICMP. On the command line: «show nve peers», «show mac address-table».
demo.datacenter.title: Data centre: leaf-spine with BGP and VXLAN
demo.datacenter.text: A data centre like those of large providers: two spines, three leafs, every leaf connected to both spines. The underlay routes with eBGP (one AS per leaf), the overlay extends VLAN 10 (web) and VLAN 20 (database) over all leafs with VXLAN.
demo.datacenter.show: First the switches set up their BGP sessions and learn the loopbacks. Then Web 1 pings Web 2 and DB 1 pings DB 2 – both within the same subnet, but across two routed hops. Filter “vxlan” or “bgp”.
demo.datacenter.tour.0: Leaf-spine is the typical design of modern data centres: every leaf is connected to every spine, every path between two servers has the same length (leaf, spine, leaf). If one spine fails, the other remains.
demo.datacenter.tour.1: The underlay is a pure IP network: every leaf–spine link is its own /30 network. Over eBGP every switch announces its loopback address. The spines have AS 65000, the leafs 65001 to 65003.
demo.datacenter.tour.2: The overlay: the leafs are VTEPs. VLAN 10 belongs to VNI 10010, VLAN 20 to VNI 10020. Each VNI only knows the leafs that have servers of that VLAN.
demo.datacenter.tour.3: In the simulation the switches report “BGP session established” one after another. Then the routing tables contain the other switches' loopbacks marked B.
demo.datacenter.tour.4: Web 1 pings Web 2. The ARP request and the ICMP travel wrapped in UDP 4789 from loopback 10.255.0.11 to 10.255.0.12 – via one of the two spines.
demo.datacenter.tour.5: DB 1 pings DB 2 over VNI 10020. Web and database stay separate: there is no gateway between the VLANs.
demo.datacenter.tour.6: In the leaf's state you see BGP neighbours, learned routes and the MAC table with the servers behind the other VTEPs. On the command line: “show ip bgp summary”, “show nve peers”.
demo.vrf.title: VRF: two customers, same addresses
demo.vrf.text: A provider router separates two customers with VRFs. Both use 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.9.0.0/24 and still never see each other.
demo.vrf.show: Both PCs open http://10.9.0.10/, the same address. Customer A gets the page of its server, customer B its own. Filter «http».
demo.vrf.tour.0: The provider router has four ports. eth0 and eth2 both have the address 10.0.0.1, eth1 and eth3 both 10.9.0.1. Without VRF this would be an error.
demo.vrf.tour.1: eth0 and eth1 belong to VRF CUSTOMER-A, eth2 and eth3 to CUSTOMER-B. Each VRF has its own routing table with only its networks.
demo.vrf.tour.2: Customer A's PC opens 10.9.0.10. The packet arrives on eth0, so the router looks in the CUSTOMER-A table and sends it via eth1 to customer A's server.
demo.vrf.tour.3: Now customer B, same address. This time the packet arrives on eth2, the CUSTOMER-B table points to eth3: customer B's page appears.
demo.vrf.tour.4: On the router's command line: «show vrf» and «show ip route vrf KUNDE-A». «show ip route» is empty because no port is in the global table.
demo.firewallZones.text: A dedicated firewall separates WAN, LAN and DMZ; an access list on the switch port lets guests reach only the web server.
demo.firewallZones.show: «Aussen» opens the web server in the DMZ (allowed) and pings the office PC (firewall blocks). Then the guest notebook pings the office PC (ACL drops) and opens the web server (allowed). Filter «tcp.port == 80 or icmp».
demo.firewallZones.tour.0: This time the firewall is a device of its own. Its ports are named after zones: eth0 is WAN, eth1 LAN, eth2 DMZ with the web server.
demo.firewallZones.tour.1: Out of the box everything may go from inside to outside, nothing from the WAN. On top is a rule of our own: HTTP to the web server, incoming on WAN. The first matching rule wins.
demo.firewallZones.tour.2: «Aussen» opens http://192.168.20.80/. Rule 1 matches, the page arrives. The firewall knows the replies from the tracked connection.
demo.firewallZones.tour.3: Now «Aussen» pings the office PC. No rule matches, the default rule denies it. The firewall's console reports the blocked packets.
demo.firewallZones.tour.4: There is also a guest notebook in the LAN. On switch port 3 the access list GAESTE checks every incoming IP packet: only HTTP to the web server is permitted, an implicit «deny» comes last.
demo.firewallZones.tour.5: The guest notebook pings the office PC in the same network. The firewall sees none of it, but the switch drops the packets right at the port. Its console shows «ACL GAESTE … dropped».
demo.firewallZones.tour.6: The web page, however, arrives: the rule matches. The replies get through because there is no ACL on the switch port towards the firewall. An ACL is stateless, it only checks what comes in on its port.
demo.firewallZones.tour.7: The office PC may go out, replies come back. Try it on the command line: «show access-lists» on the switch, «show firewall» on the firewall.
demo.vpn.title: VPN: connecting two sites
demo.vpn.text: Zürich and Bern are connected via the Internet. An IPsec tunnel between the routers turns them into one company network.
demo.vpn.show: The PC in Zürich pings the server in Bern. First the routers negotiate the tunnel with IKEv2, then packets travel encrypted in ESP. Filter «vpn».
demo.vpn.tour.0: Two sites with private networks. The Internet does not forward private addresses: without a VPN the PC in Zürich cannot reach the server in Bern.
demo.vpn.tour.1: Router Zürich has a tunnel: the peer is router Bern's public address, local network 192.168.1.0/24, remote network 192.168.2.0/24, plus a shared key.
demo.vpn.tour.2: Router Bern has the same tunnel mirrored: local and remote network are swapped, the key is the same.
demo.vpn.tour.3: The PC pings 192.168.2.20. Router Zürich notices: the destination is in the tunnel's remote network. The tunnel is not up yet, so it holds the packet and starts with IKE_SA_INIT (UDP 500).
demo.vpn.tour.4: After IKE_AUTH the tunnel is up. On the Internet you now only see ESP packets between 198.51.100.1 and 203.0.113.1 – the original with the private addresses is encrypted inside. Click an ESP packet.
demo.vpn.tour.5: The status shows «connected», plus the SPI of both sides and how many packets went through the tunnel.
demo.vpn.tour.6: A web page comes through the tunnel too. Try it yourself: re-enter the tunnel on one side with a different key and look at the console to see what happens.
demo.dsLite.tour.0: Many cable and fibre connections use DS-Lite: between you and the provider there is only IPv6. Even so, the notebook should reach websites that only speak IPv4.
demo.dsLite.tour.1: The internet box only has an IPv6 address on its WAN. Under «DS-Lite» you see the address of the AFTR at the provider. In the home network the box hands out private IPv4 addresses as usual, plus an IPv6 prefix.
demo.dsLite.tour.2: The provider acts as AFTR. It accepts the tunnels and translates the private addresses of all customers to one shared public address: 203.0.113.10. That is carrier-grade NAT.
demo.dsLite.tour.3: The notebook gets an IPv4 address from the box by DHCP and forms an IPv6 address by SLAAC. So it has both: dual stack.
demo.dsLite.tour.4: Now the notebook opens http://198.51.100.80/. Use «Single step»: the box does no NAT, it puts the whole IPv4 packet into an IPv6 packet. In single step you see layer 3 twice.
demo.dsLite.tour.5: At the provider the packet is unpacked and translated. The NAT table shows which tunnel (IPv6 address of the box) the connection came from and which public address it continues with.
demo.dsLite.tour.6: The web server only sees 203.0.113.10. That is why there is no IPv4 port forwarding with DS-Lite: the public address is not yours. Over IPv6, however, the server can be reached directly: ping 2001:db8:200::80.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: leyoNET does not process personal data: no accounts, no names, no e-mail addresses, no tracking, no advertising, no external services.
privacy.local: Projects stay on this device (in the browser storage or as a file you save yourself). Nothing is transmitted; the page technically cannot connect to the Internet.
privacy.sessions: Sessions only contain the network configuration (devices, cables, settings) under a random code. They are deleted automatically {hours} hours after the last change, or immediately with “Delete session”.
privacy.classes: Class sessions only carry a class label without personal reference (e.g. “INF22a”). Teachers see codes and results, but no names.
privacy.feedback: Feedback only contains the entered text, the program version and the language; it is deleted after {days} days.
privacy.noIp: IP addresses are neither stored nor logged. To prevent abuse, the server briefly counts requests in memory, anonymised.
privacy.storage: The browser stores only technically necessary values (session code, language, theme, feature profile, currency). There are no cookies.
privacy.rules: The concept follows the Swiss Data Protection Act (revFADP) and the EU GDPR: data minimisation, purpose limitation, short retention and privacy by design. Please do not enter names or other personal data – neither in feedback nor in device or area names – and do not upload photos of people to simulated web servers. Every release is checked automatically for privacy, security and licences.
privacy.rights: The school or person operating a web version is the controller. Sessions can be deleted by yourself at any time; the operator deletes everything else on request or automatically when the period expires.

catalog.twoPcs.title: Connect two computers

catalog.switchLan.title: Small LAN with a switch
catalog.switchLan.description: Connect all three devices to the switch and give them addresses in the same network.

catalog.switchLan.goal2: The notebook is connected to the switch.

catalog.twoSubnets.description: PC 1 and PC 2 should be in different networks and reach each other via the router. The router needs an address in each network; the PCs enter it as their default gateway.
