wire.note.tcpSeq: Sequence and acknowledgement numbers count bytes. Fixed window, no congestion control.
wire.note.sshEncrypted: Encrypted from here on: a capture shows only unreadable bytes.
wire.note.ospf: OSPFv2 per RFC 2328 with real checksums; no authentication, intra-area only.
wire.note.arp: ARP sits between layers 2 and 3: it asks for the MAC address of an IP.
wire.note.ethernet: Preamble and checksum (FCS) are omitted as in most captures; the NIC strips them.
wire.note.wlan: 802.11 management frames (simplified). Data then flows encrypted (WPA2).
wire.note.pppoe: PPPoE (RFC 2516): discovery with PADI/PADO/PADR/PADS, then a PPP session.
wire.note.docsis: DOCSIS MAC management (simplified), modulated on the coax (QAM/OFDM).
wire.note.dsLite: DS-Lite (RFC 6333): the whole IPv4 packet sits unchanged inside the IPv6 packet (next header 4). Only the AFTR at the provider unpacks it and translates the address (CGNAT).
wire.note.ike: IKEv2 (RFC 7296) on UDP 500. Real header, simplified content: no real Diffie-Hellman exchange; IKE_AUTH is encrypted (SK).
wire.note.esp: ESP (RFC 4303, IP protocol 50): SPI and sequence number are readable, the whole inner packet is encrypted. In the simulation only scrambled, no real cryptography.
wire.note.serial: Serial line: no Ethernet, no MAC addresses. Both ends need the same encapsulation.
wire.note.lte: Cellular: radio layers (PDCP/RLC/MAC) simplified; the capture contains only the IP packet.
wire.note.gpon: GPON (ITU-T G.984): PLOAM messages and GEM frames, simplified.
wire.note.adsl: ADSL2+ (ITU-T G.992.5): PPPoE over the phone line.
wire.note.vdsl: VDSL2 (ITU-T G.993.2): PPPoE over the phone line.
wire.note.phyEthernet: On the wire: preamble, frame, interframe gap.
help.overview.title: Overview
help.overview.body:
leyoNET lets you build a network from devices and cables, configure it and then run it. Devices send real packets following the standards (ARP, DHCP, DNS, TCP, HTTP, OSPF, BGP …) that you can capture and inspect layer by layer.

- Left: the **shop** with all devices ([[shop]])
- Centre: the canvas
- Right: settings of the selected item
- Top: menu bar, project name (becomes the file name when saving) and the [[modes]] switch

Everything stored is purely technical: no names, no accounts.

More space: the areas on the left (shop), right (properties) and bottom (packet list) can be hidden and shown with the grips at the edge of the canvas (‹ ›) or under **View**.
help.modes.title: Design and simulation
help.modes.body:
There are two modes; switch with **M** or **F5**.

**Design:** add devices, cable, configure and document them (areas, colour tags, descriptions, VLAN colours).

**Simulation:** the network runs. End devices ping, browse or open the command line. Devices can be moved (Wi-Fi roaming, [[roaming]]), ports shut down and packets captured ([[sniffer]]). New devices are added only in Design.

Starting the simulation creates a [[snapshots]] automatically.
help.shop.title: Shop
help.shop.body:
The shop on the left is grouped by category. Clicking a category opens its variants with ports and typical price.

- **Drag** a device onto the canvas or **click** it (placed in the centre)
- Connections: pick a type, then click two devices
- Modules: drag an SFP module onto a switch or router

What the shop shows depends on the [[features]].
help.simulation.title: Running the simulation
help.simulation.body:
- **Space** pauses or resumes, **N** takes one step. In single step the canvas has an orange frame and a notice at the top; in single step, arriving packets are unpacked layer by layer ([[osiStep]])
- Choose the speed at the top
- Double-click an end device: desktop with command prompt, browser and mail. Several desktops can be open; minimise with — and bring them back via «Open desktops» in the simulation bar. Drag a desktop by its title bar and resize it at the bottom right
- Hover over a device, cable or packet: details (addresses, tables, protocol)
- Packets visibly travel along the cables; the [[sniffer]] shows each one
- The lights on the cables: **green** connected, **orange** data in transit, **red** no connection
- Ports and cables can be shut down or damaged at any time to practise troubleshooting **Shift+N** steps back, «Reset» restarts at time 0.
help.shortcuts.title: Keyboard shortcuts
help.shortcuts.body:
**?** lists every shortcut, **Ctrl+K** (⌘K) searches any command.

- **M / F5** Design ↔ Simulation
- **V** select, **K** cable, **B** area
- **Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V** copy and paste, **Ctrl+D** duplicate, **Ctrl+A** select all ([[selection]])
- **F2** rename, **Del** delete
- **A** show IP addresses, **P** show interface names on cables, **R** rack view, **I** IP calculator
- **+ / − / 0** zoom
- **F1** help for the selected item
help.features.title: Features
help.features.body:
To keep beginners from being overwhelmed, every feature can be hidden.

- **Profile 1** starter (year-1 apprentices) up to **profile 5** university
- **Custom**: switch single features on or off
- Teachers save the selection as a file and may lock it
- In the web version the admin sets a default and a maximum profile and can lock features completely

Opening a project that uses more turns the needed features on, if allowed.
help.tasks.title: Tasks
help.tasks.body:
The **catalog** (stars = difficulty) contains ready-made exercises; each checks its goals automatically. The tabs at the top (**M117**, **M129**, **M145** …) show the exercises of one module with progress; each has a fillable worksheet (PDF). The **search field** and the **topics** (VLAN, DHCP, OSPF …) filter the list, “Only matching my profile” hides exercises that need other features. Teachers create their own under **Tools → Create task** from check blocks (ping, DHCP, route learned, questions, documentation, by hand …); «Suggest goals from this network» turns a finished solution into a task. Goals can have **points** and partial points; with «Grade» leyoNET computes the grade on the Swiss scale (5 × points / maximum + 1). When all goals are met, the catalog shows the exercise as **✓ done**. Long assignments also open in a **large window** with paragraphs, lists and highlighted commands and addresses; **⤢ Show large** opens it at any time, Esc closes it. You can keep working next to it.

**Exams:** «Tools → Save as exam» or the generator «Tools → Create exam» produce an **exam file** without checks and solutions (also one variant per seat or a **troubleshooting** exam with random faults) and a **key** for the teacher. The exam file locks catalog, editor, generator and evaluation until the teacher ends the exam with their code. **Evaluate submissions** checks all files with the key; points can be corrected by hand, reports are available for review, strikingly similar submissions are flagged.
help.webExam.title: Exams in the web version
help.webExam.body:
In the web version, exams run through the server without sending files back and forth.

**Teacher** (Tools → Admin console → Exams):
- upload the exam file and key, set seats and minutes
- **print seat cards** and hand them out: each seat has its own seat code. Who sits where is only in your seating list or on the card – the server knows no names
- **start**, give **extra time** per seat (+5′, +15′, also later), **end for everyone**
- **evaluate automatically**: all submissions corrected with the key; a **name list** (“07 Anna Example”) can be pasted into the review window and stays there only
- **download submissions**: one file with all submissions and the key, which “Review submissions” can evaluate later

**Learners:** File → Join exam … → seat code. Before the start they wait. Work is saved **every 20 seconds**; when time is up, the last saved state counts as submitted. The server deletes everything after 60 days.
help.costs.title: Costs
help.costs.body:
Every device, cable and module has a typical price. **View → Costs** shows the list and total in CHF, EUR or USD. Tasks can require a budget, which is handy for practising quotes.

Prices are indicative and exclude VAT.
help.device.notebook.title: Notebook
help.device.notebook.body: End device with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Gets its address statically or via [[dhcp]]. When on Wi-Fi it roams to the closer access point if moved during simulation ([[roaming]]).
help.device.pc.title: PC
help.device.pc.body: End device with one Ethernet port. Needs an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server ([[ip]]). Its desktop has a command prompt (ping, tracert, ipconfig, nslookup), a browser and mail.
help.device.server.title: Server
help.device.server.body: A server provides services: [[dhcp]], [[dns]], [[web]] and [[mail]]. The shop offers it empty or preconfigured. The web server serves your own pages (index.html) plus a small image. The rack variant fits into a [[racks]].
help.device.clientgroup.title: Client group
help.device.clientgroup.body:
Stands for many identical clients (2 to 500), e.g. a classroom with 25 PCs. All get their address via [[dhcp]], so the subnet and DHCP pool must be large enough.

During simulation you can pick a single member to ping from. It counts multiple times in the cost.
help.device.switch.title: Switch
help.device.switch.body:
Connects devices in the same network. It learns which MAC address is on which port and forwards frames accordingly ([[switching]]). Managed switches support [[vlan]], [[trunk]] and [[stp]]. SFP slots accept fibre modules ([[sfp]]).

**Management address:** with the VLAN feature the switch has a VLAN interface in the **Addresses** tab, reachable by ping and SSH (`interface vlan 1`, `ip address …`, `ip default-gateway …`). It does not route.
help.device.l3switch.title: Layer 3 switch
help.device.l3switch.body: A switch that also routes: one virtual interface (SVI) with an IP address per VLAN acts as the gateway. VLANs can then talk without an external router. With IPv6 every SVI also gets an IPv6 address and announces its prefix in the VLAN ([[ipv6]]).
help.device.router.title: Router
help.device.router.body:
Connects different networks; each interface sits in a different one. The router uses its routing table ([[routing]]) to decide where a packet goes.

- Ports as **Ethernet** or **serial** ([[serial]])
- [[nat]], [[staticNat]], [[portForward]]
- dynamic routing: [[ospf]], [[rip]], [[bgp]]
- DHCP relay and subinterfaces ([[routerOnAStick]])
help.device.accesspoint.title: Access point
help.device.accesspoint.body: Creates a Wi-Fi network (SSID, band, channel, password). Clients join via 802.11 (authentication, association, 4-way handshake). Several access points with the same SSID allow [[roaming]]; APs linked wirelessly form a mesh.
help.device.modem.title: Modem
help.device.modem.body: Connects your network to the provider over an access line ([[access]]). Types: cable (DOCSIS over coax), fibre (GPON ONT), mobile (LTE/5G), ADSL or VDSL (PPPoE over the phone line). The line set-up appears in the packet list.
help.device.cpe.title: Internet box (CPE)
help.device.cpe.body:
The internet box (CPE, customer premises equipment) is the device the provider installs at home. It combines modem, router, NAT, DHCP server and a small switch:

- **WAN**: access line to the provider (cable, fibre, VDSL … or Ethernet). With an access technology it first sets up the line ([[access]]).
- **LAN 1–4**: one shared network, factory default 192.168.1.1/24. Computers get their address via DHCP (192.168.1.100–199).
- **NAT**: all computers appear on the internet with the WAN address ([[nat]]).

You only enter the WAN address and the provider's gateway. Everything else (DHCP range, port forwarding, routes) is under «Advanced …».
help.advanced.title: Advanced settings
help.advanced.body:
The inspector on the right shows only the basic settings: name, addresses, the SSID for an access point. **Advanced …** (key **E**) opens everything else in a separate window with tabs:

- **General**, **Addresses**, **Ports** (front view and port table)
- **Routing**: routing table coloured by origin (C connected, S static, S* default route, O OSPF, R RIP, B BGP). Enter a new route in the last row and add it with +
- depending on the device **NAT**, **DHCP**, **VLAN & STP**, **Wi-Fi**, **Email**, **Services**, **Access**
- in the simulation also **State** (ARP, MAC and NAT tables)

The window can be moved by its header and resized at the bottom right. Each device can have its own window (up to six) while the canvas stays usable. ◀ ▶ or **Page Up/Page Down** switches straight to the previous or next device; the tab stays.

Input is saved as soon as you leave a field (Tab, click elsewhere or Enter). Errors only appear when you leave the form so that half-finished input does not get in the way.
help.demos.title: Demo networks
help.demos.body:
**File → Demo networks …** (or ▶ in the toolbar) offers a ready-made network for every protocol: ARP and ping, gateway, DHCP, DNS/TCP/HTTP, email, VLAN and STP, broadcast storm, router on a stick, layer 3 switch, automatic routing, static routes, OSPF, RIP, BGP, NAT, SNAT, DNAT, internet box, serial line with PPP and Wi-Fi mesh.

- **Present** starts the simulation and triggers the matching action (e.g. a ping) with the desktop open
- **Step by step** (for many demos): an avatar teacher explains the test case in small steps, highlights devices, opens the matching settings and pauses the simulation so you can follow along in single step. Everyone can customise the avatar (click the avatar or **Help → Customise avatar …**); only the appearance is saved, only in your own browser. — (or Esc) hides the speech bubble; the avatar stays small in the corner and brings it back with one click. A finished tour can also be shown again via **Help → Show the teacher** or in the demo networks.
- **Open** loads the network into design mode to explore and change

**Undo** brings back the previous project. Every demo is checked automatically with each release.
help.selection.title: Select, move, copy
help.selection.body:
In **design** mode you can work on several devices and areas at once:

- **Selection frame:** drag on empty space. Every device whose centre lies inside the frame is selected, and every area that lies completely inside it. With **Shift** the frame adds to the current selection and can also be drawn inside an area.
- **Shift+click** adds or removes a device or area, **Ctrl+A** selects everything on the floor shown.
- **Moving:** dragging a selected item moves the whole selection; so do the arrow keys (further with Shift). An area only moves itself; the devices inside it only move along if they are selected too (e.g. with a frame around everything).
- **Copy and paste:** **Ctrl+C** copies, **Ctrl+V** pastes with an offset (again and again, each time further along), **Ctrl+D** duplicates directly. Cables between the selected devices are copied too, cables to the outside are not. A single device comes without IP addresses because it usually belongs in the same network. A group keeps all its settings, e.g. for a second branch office. If it later ends up in the same network, leyoNET warns about duplicate addresses ([[duplicates]]).
- **Del** deletes the whole selection, **Undo** brings it back.

**Panning the view:** drag with the right or middle mouse button, or hold **Space** and drag. In the simulation, dragging on empty space also pans. The mouse wheel zooms.
help.osiStep.title: Single step with OSI layers
help.osiStep.body:
When paused, each packet shows its layers nested inside each other, each in its colour (shown at the bottom). **Single step** (N) unpacks an arriving packet at the receiver layer by layer, and the colour changes:

- **Switch, access point, modem** up to layer 2: they read the destination MAC and forward
- **Router** up to layer 3: read the destination IP, look up the route, forward (fully unpacked if the packet is for the router itself)
- **End device**: fully if the packet is for it; with another destination MAC it is dropped at layer 2

Only after the last layer does the device process the packet. **Resume** (Space) continues normally.
help.duplicates.title: Duplicate addresses
help.duplicates.body:
If two devices in the same network have the same IP address, a red **!** appears on the device, the address turns red and the form shows a warning. In the simulation, addresses obtained via DHCP count too.

The same network means: connected through cables, switches, access points or modems without a router in between. Behind different routers (e.g. two home networks with 192.168.1.1) the same private address is fine.
help.device.internet.title: Internet
help.device.internet.body: Represents the provider and the rest of the Internet: public addresses, a DNS server and websites like example.com. The provider can give customers [[cgnat]] addresses.
help.cables.title: Cables and links
help.cables.body:
- **TP cable** (copper, RJ45) for most connections
- **Fibre** between SFP modules ([[sfp]])
- **Wi-Fi** to the access point ([[wlan]])
- **Serial** between routers ([[serial]])
- **Coax, DSL, cellular** from the modem or internet box to the provider ([[access]])

**Choosing the port:** when connecting, the simulator plugs the cable into the next free port. With «Port: choose from list» (at the top of the canvas) a list of ports appears instead; ports in use show what they are connected to.

**Interface names** (e.g. Gi0/1) at the cable ends can be shown or hidden under **View** or with **P**.

If the type does not fit the port, the simulator tells you. Cables can be damaged and ports shut down in the simulation.
help.sfp.title: SFP modules
help.sfp.body: SFP slots take modules that decide which fibre fits: **SX/SR** for multimode (short runs in a building), **LX/LR** for single-mode (up to 10 km). Both ends need the same module type. Routers and switches come **without** SFP slots: set the number under “General” in the window, or simply drag a module from the palette onto the device – the slot is then added automatically.
help.serial.title: Serial lines
help.serial.body:
Classic WAN line between two routers. No Ethernet, no MAC addresses; there is only one neighbour, so no ARP is needed.

- Switch the router port to **serial**
- Same **encapsulation** on both ends: HDLC (Cisco) or PPP
- PPP negotiates the link with LCP and the addresses with IPCP

In the CLI: `interface serial0`, `encapsulation ppp`.
help.wlan.title: Wi-Fi
help.wlan.body: A client joins an access point when SSID and password match and it is in range. Signal strength depends on distance. The packet list shows the join: authentication, association and the WPA2 EAPOL 4-way handshake.
help.roaming.title: Roaming
help.roaming.body: When you move a Wi-Fi device during simulation, it checks signal strength. If another access point with the same SSID is clearly closer (at least 10 percentage points stronger), it reassociates there and sends a gratuitous ARP so switches learn the new path.
help.access.title: Access lines
help.access.body:
The modem sets up the line to the provider according to its standard:

- **Cable (DOCSIS):** channel scan, ranging, config via TFTP, registration
- **Fibre (GPON):** serial number, ONU ID via PLOAM, config via OMCI
- **Mobile (LTE):** RRC, attach with SIM, bearer with IP
- **ADSL/VDSL:** training (G.hs), then PPPoE and PPP with user and password

Only then do IP packets flow.
help.ip.title: IP addresses
help.ip.body:
Every device needs an **IP address** and a **mask** (e.g. 192.168.1.10/24). The mask says which part is the network. If the destination is in another network, the device sends the packet to its **gateway** (the router). The **DNS server** turns names into addresses.

See also [[subnetting]], [[scopes]] and [[ipcalc]].

Values are saved as soon as you leave the field (Tab, Enter or clicking elsewhere, including another device). If the mask is missing, leyoNET fills in the usual mask of the address class (e.g. /24 for 192.168.x.x); you can change it at any time.
help.subnetting.title: Subnetting
help.ipv6.title: IPv6
help.ipv6.body:
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long and written as eight blocks of four hex digits, e.g. **2001:db8:1::10/64**. Leading zeros are dropped, one run of zero blocks becomes **::** (RFC 5952). **2001:db8::/32** is reserved for examples, private networks use **fd00::/8**.

**IP version of the project** (at the top of the toolbar): **IPv4** (as before), **v4 + v6** (dual stack, both at once) or **IPv6** (IPv4 switched off).

- **Link-local:** every IPv6 interface automatically has an address **fe80::…** formed from the MAC (EUI-64). It is only valid on its own link.
- **Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP:** to find the MAC for an address, a device sends a **Neighbor Solicitation** to a multicast group; the owner answers with a **Neighbor Advertisement**. Before using an address, every device checks that it is free (**DAD**). `netsh interface ipv6 show neighbors` lists the neighbours.
- **SLAAC:** routers send **router advertisements** with their prefix (/64). End devices set to “IPv6 automatic” form their own address from it and take the router as default gateway.
- **DHCPv6:** if “Hand out addresses by DHCPv6” is set on the router port, the router advertisement carries the M flag and end devices get their address by Solicit – Advertise – Request – Reply.
- **Layer 3 switch:** every VLAN interface (SVI) gets an IPv6 address and announces its prefix in the VLAN (also over trunks). The switch routes between the VLANs; with “no ip routing” it does not.
- **Routing:** connected prefixes, static routes (Routing tab → IPv6 routes) or [[autoRouting]].
- **Ping and tracert** work with IPv6 addresses, `ipconfig` shows all addresses.
- **DNS over IPv6:** a **DNS server** can be set on the router port. It is carried in the router advertisement (RDNSS option, RFC 8106) and in the DHCPv6 reply; end devices with a fixed address enter it themselves. **AAAA** records return IPv6 addresses.
- **Applications:** ping, tracert, browser, e-mail and SSH work over IPv6, by address or by name. In dual stack, a device with a global IPv6 address uses the AAAA record first, otherwise the A record. In URLs an IPv6 address goes in square brackets: `http://[2001:db8:1::80]/`.

Dynamic routing for IPv6: [[ospf6]] and [[ripng]].

Simplified: no MLD, no extension headers, no privacy addresses, no NAT for IPv6.
help.subnetting.body: A network can be split into smaller subnets by lengthening the prefix: 192.168.1.0/24 becomes two /25 or four /26. Each subnet loses two addresses (network and broadcast). With VLSM each subnet gets exactly the size it needs. The [[ipcalc]] does both.
help.ipcalc.title: IP calculator
help.ipcalc.body: Press **I** or the button next to an address field. It shows network, broadcast, first and last host, host count, wildcard and binary. Below it splits a network evenly or by need (VLSM). **Apply** writes the values straight into the device.
help.scopes.title: Private and public addresses
help.scopes.body:
- **Private** (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16): local only, to the Internet via [[nat]]
- **CGNAT** (100.64/10): assigned by the provider, who translates again ([[cgnat]])
- **Public:** globally unique

Press **A** to show all addresses in colour. A «Public network» area marks networks with public addresses, e.g. a DMZ.
help.dhcp.title: DHCP
help.dhcp.body: A DHCP server hands out addresses in four steps: **Discover** (client broadcasts), **Offer**, **Request**, **Ack**. The server supplies address, mask, gateway and DNS. If the server is in another network, a router with **DHCP relay** forwards the requests. With a **fixed assignment** (reservation), a specific device, recognised by its MAC address, always gets the same address, e.g. a printer or a workstation; it may also lie outside the range. **DHCP pools** on a router or layer 3 switch (“DHCP” tab, “ip dhcp pool”): one pool per network with network, gateway and DNS; excluded addresses (“ip dhcp excluded-address”) are never handed out.
help.dns.title: DNS
help.dns.body:
DNS translates names into addresses and back. The client asks its DNS server via UDP port 53 and caches the answer for its TTL (`ipconfig /displaydns`, `ipconfig /flushdns`).

- **A** and **AAAA**: name → IPv4 or IPv6 address
- **CNAME**: alias for another name (the server follows the chain)
- **MX**: mail server of a domain; the smallest preference wins
- **TXT**: text, e.g. an SPF rule
- **NS**: name server of the domain
- **PTR**: address → name (reverse lookup under in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa)

The server answers names in its own zone **authoritatively**. With **forwarding** it asks another server (e.g. the provider's) for all other names and answers “non-authoritative”. Test with `nslookup -type=MX school.example`, `nslookup 192.168.0.3` (PTR) or `nslookup name server` (ask a specific server).
help.switching.title: Switching
help.switching.body: A switch records each frame's source MAC and port (MAC table). If it knows the destination it forwards only there, otherwise to all ports (flooding). Broadcasts such as ARP always go to every port in the same VLAN. If two devices share a MAC address, the switch learns it alternately on two ports («MAC flapping»): frames reach the wrong device and the switch console reports «MAC moves».
help.vlan.title: VLANs
help.vlan.body:
VLANs split one switch into separate networks. An **access port** belongs to exactly one VLAN, a **trunk** carries several ([[trunk]]).

Under **Tools → VLANs** each VLAN gets a name and a colour. The colour automatically tints every port of that VLAN on the canvas and in the port table. Between VLANs you need a router ([[routerOnAStick]]) or a layer 3 switch.

**Creating VLANs:** a switch only forwards VLANs it knows (tab **Switching → VLANs on this switch** or `vlan 20`, `name Training`). Assigning a new VLAN to an access port creates it, as on Cisco. A switch in the middle with trunks only still needs the VLANs, otherwise it drops the frames (console: «VLAN 20 is not created»). `no vlan 20` deletes a VLAN, its ports become inactive. Files before version 1.2 have no list: there all VLANs in use count as created.
help.trunk.title: Trunks
help.trunk.body:
A trunk links switches (or switch and router) and carries several VLANs on one cable. Each frame gets an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN number; the **native VLAN** runs untagged.

**Allowed VLANs:** by default a trunk carries all created VLANs. With `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20` only these; `… add 30`, `… remove 10`, `… except 1`, `… all`, `… none`. `switchport trunk native vlan 99` changes the untagged VLAN (set it the same on both sides). `show interfaces trunk` shows allowed and active VLANs per trunk. In the form, native VLAN and allowed VLANs are in the port table.
help.stp.title: Spanning tree (STP)
help.stp.body:
Redundant cables between switches form loops. Without STP, broadcasts circulate forever: a **broadcast storm** that cripples the network. The simulator then shows a warning and the affected devices.

With STP the switches elect a root bridge and block some ports until a path fails. Enable it on the switch under «Spanning tree».
help.lag.title: Port-channel (link aggregation)
help.lag.body:
A **port-channel** bundles several cables between two switches into one logical link: more bandwidth and redundancy, without a loop. Spanning tree sees the channel as one port.

- Put the same ports into a channel on **both** switches (tab **Switching**, column port-channel, or `channel-group 1 mode active`).
- **LACP** (IEEE 802.1AX) negotiates the bundle: at least one side must be **active**, the other may be **passive**. **On** bundles without negotiation; if the other side is set up wrongly, a loop results.
- All ports of a channel need the same VLAN or trunk setting; differing ports are suspended. `interface port-channel 1` configures all of them at once.
- If a port leads to a different switch or the other side has no channel, it stays suspended (no loop).
- Each conversation takes one cable depending on the MAC addresses; if one fails, all continue over the rest.

`show etherchannel summary` shows the state (P bundled, s suspended). Several cables without a channel form a loop: see [[stp]].
help.vxlan.title: VXLAN
help.vxlan.body:
**VXLAN** (RFC 7348) extends a VLAN across a routed network. A **VTEP** (here a layer-3 switch) wraps every frame of the VLAN including its MAC addresses in a UDP packet (port 4789) with the **VNI**, a 24-bit number for the segment, and sends it by IP to the other VTEPs.

- Link VLAN and VNI: in the VLAN `vn-segment 10010`.
- Tunnel source: usually a [[loopback]] (`interface nve1`, `source-interface loopback0`), reachable in the underlay via OSPF or statically.
- Enter the other VTEPs as a fixed list (ingress replication): `member vni 10010 peer-ip 10.255.0.2`. Broadcasts and unknown destinations go to all, learned MAC addresses only to their VTEP («flood and learn»).
- Frames from VTEPs not in the list are dropped.

In the form: tab **Switching**, section VXLAN. Display: `show nve vni`, `show nve peers`, `show mac address-table` (entries «nve1»). **EVPN** (BGP distributes the MAC addresses) is not modelled.
help.loopback.title: Loopback interfaces
help.loopback.body:
A **loopback** is an interface without a cable that is always up. Usually it has a /32 address (e.g. 10.255.0.1/32).

- **Router ID:** OSPF takes the highest loopback address, otherwise the highest interface address.
- OSPF advertises a loopback as a host route (/32) and sends no hellos there.
- Fixed management address: reachable as long as any path to the device exists.
- Source of tunnels, e.g. [[vxlan]].

Router, firewall and layer-3 switch; in the **Addresses** tab or on the command line: `interface loopback0`, `ip address 10.255.0.1/32`, `no interface loopback0`.
help.vrf.title: VRF
help.vrf.body:
**VRF** (virtual routing and forwarding) gives a router several separate routing tables. Typical at a provider: customer A and customer B both use 10.0.0.0/24, run through the same router and still never see each other.

- Every port (also subinterface, VLAN interface, loopback) belongs to the **global** table or to a VRF.
- A packet stays in the VRF of the port it arrives on. Replies of the router (ping) go back into the same VRF.
- Each VRF has its directly connected networks and its own **static routes**. OSPF, RIP, BGP, NAT and automatic routing only work in the global table.

In the form: tab **VRF**. Command line:

- `vrf definition CUSTOMER-A`
- on the interface `vrf forwarding CUSTOMER-A`
- `ip route vrf CUSTOMER-A 0.0.0.0/0 10.1.1.2`
- `show vrf`, `show ip route vrf CUSTOMER-A`, `ping vrf CUSTOMER-A 10.9.0.10`
help.routerOnAStick.title: Router on a stick
help.routerOnAStick.body: A router with a single cable to the switch routes between VLANs: the switch port is a trunk and the router has one **subinterface** per VLAN (e.g. eth0.10) with its own IP as gateway.
help.routing.title: Routing
help.routing.body:
The routing table says via which neighbour a network is reachable. Entries come from:

- **connected** networks
- **automatic routing** for beginners: the router calculates its routes by itself ([[autoRouting]])
- **static** routes, entered by hand
- **dynamic** protocols: [[ospf]], [[rip]], [[bgp]]

The most specific route wins (longest prefix); ties go to the lower administrative distance (connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, RIP 120, iBGP 200).
help.autoRouting.title: Automatic routing
help.autoRouting.body:
To get started: tick **Automatic routing** on the router (or layer 3 switch), on the right in the properties or in the **Routing** tab. The router then knows every network in the plan without entering any routes.

- For each network it takes the path through the **fewest routers**. Neighbours are routers whose ports are in the same network (cable or switch in between, same subnet).
- If a path leads to the **internet** (provider or internet box), a **default route** towards it is added.
- In the routing table these routes are marked **A** (automatic). In design mode the **Routing** tab shows a preview.
- If you shut down a port, automatic routing looks for another path if there is one.
- Every router needs the tick itself: a router without a matching route drops the packet, even if the others route automatically.

This is a shortcut of the simulator, not a real protocol. In real networks, static routes or protocols such as [[ospf]] and [[rip]] do this job.

**Without the tick** you choose:
- **Static:** enter every route by hand.
- **Dynamic:** the routers exchange their networks using OSPF, RIP or BGP; static routes apply as well.

Routes and protocols you have entered stay saved when you switch. They are only inactive while another mode is chosen.
help.ospf.title: OSPF
help.ospf.body:
OSPF is a link-state protocol: each router describes its links (LSA), all collect the map and compute shortest paths with Dijkstra.

- **Hello** finds neighbours (standard every 10 s, shortened to 2 s in the simulator) (multicast 224.0.0.5)
- **DBD, LSR, LSU, LSAck** synchronise the database until the neighbour is **Full**
- Cost per interface (default 10), adjustable with `ip ospf cost`

CLI: `router ospf`, `network 10.0.0.0/24 area 0` (or with wildcard `0.0.0.255`), `show ip ospf neighbor`.
help.rip.title: RIP
help.rip.body: RIP v2 is a distance-vector protocol: routers regularly send their whole table to neighbours (standard every 30 s, shortened to 5 s in the simulator) (UDP 520, multicast 224.0.0.9). The metric is the hop count; 16 means unreachable. Simple but slow to converge.
help.ospf6.title: OSPFv3 (IPv6)
help.ospf6.body:
OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) is OSPF for IPv6. The process is the same as for [[ospf]]: hello, DBD, LSR, LSU, LSAck, then **full** and Dijkstra. Differences:

- Routers talk over their **link-local addresses**; hellos go to **ff02::5**, IPv6 next header 89.
- You add **interfaces**, not networks (in FRRouting `ipv6 ospf6 area 0` on the interface).
- The **router ID** stays a 32-bit number written like an IPv4 address. If a router has no IPv4 address you should set it (otherwise the simulator derives one from the MAC).
- Router LSAs only describe the links; the networks are carried in **intra-area prefix LSAs**.
- The next hop in the routing table is the neighbour’s link-local address.

CLI: `router ospf6`, `ospf6 router-id 1.1.1.1`, `interface eth0 area 0`, `show ipv6 ospf6 neighbor`, `show ipv6 ospf6 database`, `show ipv6 route` (code O). Layer 3 switches speak OSPFv3 on their VLAN interfaces.

Simplified like OSPFv2: no DR/BDR election, no network and link LSAs, one area.
help.ripng.title: RIPng (IPv6)
help.ripng.body:
RIPng (RFC 2080) is [[rip]] for IPv6: routers send their table regularly (every 5 s in the simulator) by **UDP 521** to **ff02::9**, with their link-local address as source and hop limit 255. The metric is the number of routers; 16 means unreachable. Split horizon as with RIP v2.

CLI: `router ripng`, `network eth0` (interface instead of network), `redistribute connected`, `default-information originate`, `show ipv6 ripng`, `show ipv6 route` (code R).
help.bgp.title: BGP
help.bgp.body:
BGP connects **autonomous systems** (AS) such as providers and companies. Neighbours are configured by hand and talk over TCP port 179: **OPEN**, **KEEPALIVE**, then **UPDATE** with announced networks and the AS path.

- **eBGP** between different ASes, **iBGP** within one
- The shortest AS path wins

CLI: `router bgp 65001`, `neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65002`, `show ip bgp summary`.
help.nat.title: NAT/PAT
help.nat.body:
Private addresses are not reachable on the internet. NAT therefore replaces addresses between inside and outside. There are two directions:

- **SNAT** (source NAT) replaces the **source address** of outgoing packets. The most common form is **PAT** (masquerading): everyone shares the router address and is told apart by port. With **static SNAT** a device always goes out with a fixed public address. Replies come back through the remembered connection, new connections from outside do not.
- **DNAT** (destination NAT) replaces the **destination address** of incoming packets: as a [[portForward]] (one port) or as **static DNAT** (a whole public address). The replies leave the router with the public address again.

**1:1 NAT** combines both ([[staticNat]]). Everything is set in the **NAT** tab of the advanced settings; in the simulation the NAT table shows the type of each entry. See also [[cgnat]].
help.firewall.title: Firewall
help.firewall.body:
A **firewall** decides for every packet: let it through or drop it. It checks the rules **from top to bottom**; the **first match** wins. If none matches, the **default rule** applies. The safe choice is «deny everything not allowed» (default rule *Deny*).

A rule consists of:

- **action**: Allow or Deny
- **protocol** (TCP, UDP, ICMP or any) and for TCP/UDP the **destination port**, e.g. 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 53 for DNS
- **source** and **destination**: `any`, an address or a network such as `192.168.1.0/24`
- on a router optionally the **inbound** interface (where the packet arrives)

**Stateful** inspection: the firewall remembers allowed connections. Replies come back without a rule of their own. Turn it off and the return direction needs a rule too – this shows why stateful firewalls exist.

**Routers** filter forwarded packets (after DNAT, before SNAT), **end devices** filter incoming packets (host firewall). Configure it in the **Firewall** tab of the advanced settings. In the simulation, counters show how often each rule matched; blocked packets appear in the console. A typical setup: a **DMZ** with the web server, only port 80/443 open from outside. See also [[nat]], [[vpn]] and [[acl]].

**Own device:** the [[device.firewall]] from the shop filters out of the box. **Command line** on router and firewall: `firewall default deny`, `firewall rule allow tcp any 192.168.2.80 port 80 in eth0` (a number first inserts at that position), `no firewall rule 2`, `no firewall stateful`, `show firewall`. Switches use access lists instead: [[acl]].
help.acl.title: Access lists (ACL)
help.acl.body:
An **access list** (access control list, ACL) filters the IP packets that **arrive** on a port of a **switch**. On a **layer 3 switch** also on the VLAN interface: `in` checks everything from the VLAN (also to the switch itself, e.g. DHCP to the relay), `out` everything routed into the VLAN. This separates guests from the internal server, for example, without building a separate network.

- Rules are checked **from top to bottom**, the **first match** wins.
- An **implicit deny** comes last: whatever no rule allows is dropped.
- **Stateless:** unlike the [[firewall]], the ACL does not remember connections. Replies are checked on the port they arrive on.
- ARP, spanning tree and IPv6 neighbour discovery always pass.
- An ACL only takes effect once it is applied to a port. If the name is applied but the list was deleted, everything passes.

In the form: advanced settings of the switch, tab **ACL**. On the **command line** as on Cisco:

- `ip access-list extended GUESTS`
- `permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.10.80 eq 80`
- `deny ip any any` (implicit at the end anyway)
- `no 20` removes the entry with number 20
- on the port: `interface port1`, `ip access-group GUESTS in`
- `show access-lists` shows the matches in the simulation

Addresses: `any`, `host A`, `A W` with a wildcard mask (0.0.0.255 = /24) or `A/24`.
help.device.firewall.title: Firewall
help.device.firewall.body:
A **firewall** as a device of its own: it routes like a router but filters out of the box. The ports are named after their **zone**:

- **eth0 (WAN)**: to the internet or provider
- **eth1 (LAN)**: internal network
- **eth2 (DMZ)**: servers that should be reachable from outside
- **eth3 … (OPT)**: further zones

**Out of the box:** stateful, LAN, DMZ and OPT may go out, everything else is denied. Replies come back, new connections from the WAN need a rule of their own, e.g. «Allow TCP 80 to the web server, incoming on WAN». Unlike a router it uses the same rules to protect **itself**: out of the box it answers neither ping nor SSH from the WAN (packets from its own VPN peers are exempt).

Configure it in the **Firewall** tab or on the command line (`firewall rule allow tcp any 192.168.2.80 port 80 in wan`, `show firewall`). Besides that it can do everything a router can: [[nat]], [[portForward]], [[vpn]], static and dynamic routes. See [[firewall]].
help.vpn.title: VPN (IPsec)
help.vpn.body:
A **site-to-site VPN** connects two sites over the Internet as if they were in the same company network. The routers set up an encrypted **IPsec tunnel**.

On **both** routers a tunnel is entered in the **VPN** tab:

- **peer**: public address of the other router
- **local network** and **remote network** – exactly mirrored on the other side
- **pre-shared key**, the same on both sides

The first packet to the remote network starts the negotiation with **IKEv2** (UDP 500): first **IKE_SA_INIT** (algorithms and key material), then **IKE_AUTH** (both prove they know the key and agree on the networks). If the key does not match, authentication fails.

After that, packets travel in **ESP** (IP protocol 50): outside the public router addresses, inside the whole original packet, encrypted. The packet list and the OSI window show both headers; a capture on the Internet shows only unreadable bytes. NAT does not apply to tunnel traffic, and the remote network needs no route.

Simplified: no real cryptography, no rekeying, no NAT traversal. Filters: `esp`, `ike`, `vpn`. See also [[firewall]].
help.staticNat.title: 1:1 NAT (static NAT)
help.staticNat.body:
Maps an inside address to a fixed outside address, in both directions: outgoing, the router replaces the source address (**SNAT**), incoming the destination address (**DNAT**). That way a server is reachable under its own public address and also goes out with it. The router answers ARP requests for the outside address (proxy ARP).

If only one direction should apply, the NAT tab offers **static SNAT** or **static DNAT** ([[nat]]).

CLI: `ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10` (1:1 only).
help.portForward.title: Port forwarding
help.portForward.body: Forwards requests to a port on the public address (e.g. TCP 80) to a device in the private network, making a web server behind NAT reachable from outside. It doesn't work behind [[cgnat]] because the public address belongs to the provider.
help.cgnat.title: Carrier-grade NAT
help.dsLite.title: DS-Lite
help.dsLite.body:
**DS-Lite** (Dual-Stack Lite, RFC 6333) carries IPv4 across a provider network that only speaks IPv6. Many cable and fibre connections work this way.

- The **internet box** (B4) only has an IPv6 address on its WAN. It puts IPv4 from the home network unchanged into an IPv6 packet (next header 4) and sends it to the provider's **AFTR**. It does no NAT itself.
- The **AFTR** unpacks the IPv4 packet and translates the private source address by **CGNAT** to a public address shared by many customers. Replies take the reverse path back through the tunnel.
- That is why you cannot set up IPv4 port forwarding with DS-Lite: the public IPv4 address does not belong to the customer. Over IPv6, however, the devices can be reached directly.

Setting it up: project on **v4 + v6**; on the internet box the WAN IPv6 address and, under DS-Lite, the address of the AFTR; at the provider “Act as AFTR” and a CGNAT address. In the packet list, the filter `dslite` shows the tunnelled packets.
help.cgnat.body: Because IPv4 addresses are scarce, many providers give customers only an address from 100.64.0.0/10 and translate to public addresses themselves. The customer then has double NAT and cannot forward ports. Enable it on the Internet device per customer port.
help.web.title: Web server and browser
help.web.body: The web server serves your own pages: edit index.html and upload a small image (it is shrunk, at most 160 kB, so the project file stays small). The browser resolves the name via DNS, opens a TCP connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), sends GET and then loads embedded images. All per HTTP/1.1.
help.mail.title: E-mail
help.mail.body: A mail server accepts messages via **SMTP** (port 25). They are fetched via **POP3** (110, download) or **IMAP** (143, keep on server). The sender finds the mail server through the MX record in DNS.
help.cli.title: Command line
help.cli.body:
Routers, firewalls and switches can be configured on the command line (modelled on Cisco IOS and FRRouting). Open it: double-click the device or “Command line” in its window. Everything you set in the CLI appears in the forms and vice versa.

**Usage:** `Tab` completes, `?` shows the options, `↑`/`↓` recalls earlier commands (kept until reload, also when switching between design and simulation). **Right-click pastes**; several lines (e.g. a whole `show running-config`) run one after another. Abbreviations like `conf t`, `int g0/0`, `sh ip ro` work. A command of another level (e.g. `interface vlan 10` while in `router ospf`) jumps there.

**Modes:** `enable` (privileged), `configure terminal` (configuration), `interface …`, `vlan …`, `router ospf 1`, `ip dhcp pool …`, `ip access-list extended …`; `exit` one level up, `end` all the way out.

**`do`:** run a show command from configuration mode without leaving it: `do show ip interface brief`, `do ping 192.168.1.1`, `do write`.

**Examples:**
- Address: `interface eth0` → `ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0` → `no shutdown`
- VLAN and access port: `vlan 10` → `name ENTWICKLUNG` → `interface port1` → `switchport access vlan 10`
- Trunk: `interface port8` → `switchport mode trunk` → `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20`
- Router on a stick: `interface eth0.10` → `encapsulation dot1q 10` → `ip address 192.168.10.1/24`
- Layer 3 switch: `ip routing` → `interface vlan 10` → `ip address 192.168.10.1/24` → `ip helper-address 192.168.20.200`
- Static route: `ip route 10.0.0.0 255.0.0.0 192.168.1.254`
- OSPF: `router ospf 1` → `network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0`
- DHCP pool: `ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.9` → `ip dhcp pool VLAN10` → `network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0` → `default-router 192.168.10.1`
- ACL: `ip access-list extended GAST` → `permit tcp any host 192.168.1.80 eq 80` → `interface port2` → `ip access-group GAST in`
- Port channel: `interface range port7 - 8` → `channel-group 1 mode active`
- Checks: `show running-config`, `show ip route`, `show vlan brief`, `show interfaces trunk`, `show ip ospf neighbor`, `show access-lists`, `show ip dhcp binding`, `show etherchannel summary`

All commands: documentation `docs/cli.md`.
help.ssh.title: SSH
help.ssh.body: With SSH (TCP 22) you log in from a PC to a router or switch and configure it remotely. After the key exchange everything is encrypted; a capture shows only unreadable bytes.
help.sniffer.title: Packet list
help.sniffer.body: The packet list shows every frame crossing a cable: time, path, protocol, source, destination and a summary. Clicking opens the details following the [[osi]] model. Use the [[filter]] to hide what you don't need, and [[pcap]] to take the capture into Wireshark. **Each packet once** hides unchanged forwards by switches; turn it off to see every segment.
help.osi.title: OSI model
help.osi.body:
Each frame is encoded into real bytes and broken down by layer: application (7) at the top, wire (1) at the bottom. Each layer wraps the one above: HTTP inside TCP, TCP inside IP, IP inside Ethernet.

- Empty layers are greyed out (e.g. ARP has no layer 3 or 4)
- Clicking a field highlights its bytes in the hex view
- Checksums are computed for real
help.filter.title: Display filter
help.filter.body:
The filter works much like Wireshark's:

- protocols: `arp`, `dhcp`, `dns`, `http`, `icmp`, `tcp`, `udp`, `stp`, `ospf`, `rip`, `bgp`, `ppp`, `wlan`, `broadcast`, IPv6: `ipv6`, `icmpv6`, `ndp`, `dhcpv6`, `dslite`, VPN: `esp`, `ike`, `vpn`, data centre: `vxlan`, `lacp`
- comparisons: `ip.addr == 10.0.0.1`, `ip.src`, `ip.dst`, `ipv6.addr`, `ipv6.src`, `ipv6.dst`, `eth.addr`, `port == 80`, `tcp.port`, `udp.port`, `vlan == 10`, `tcp.stream == 0` (one TCP connection), `tcp.flags.syn == 1` (also `ack`, `fin`, `rst`), also with `!=`
- `host PC1` (device name), `lost` (lost frames)
- combine with `and`, `or`, `not` and parentheses
- **Follow TCP stream:** click a packet, then “Follow TCP stream”. The list shows only that connection (like “Follow TCP Stream” in Wireshark); the bar on top shows whether setup (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), data and teardown (FIN) occurred.

Example: `dhcp or (icmp and host PC1)`. The chips below the filter set common expressions.
help.pcap.title: pcap export
help.pcap.body: **File → Export capture** saves all frames as a pcapng file. Wireshark opens it like a real capture; each link appears as its own interface with the right link type (Ethernet, PPP, Wi-Fi …).
help.areas.title: Areas
help.areas.body:
Areas document the network: subnets, VLANs, rooms, zones and public networks. Draw with **B** or drag from the shop. A VLAN area takes the VLAN's colour. Dragging moves only the area; devices inside come along if they are selected too. Select several areas and devices with a frame ([[selection]]).

**Text box:** in the shop under **Areas → Text box** there is a box for free text: info, assignment, legend. Blank line = new paragraph, «- » = list, **bold**, `command`; IP addresses are highlighted. The text shows right on the canvas, the bottom right corner enlarges the box.
help.racks.title: Racks
help.racks.body: Switches, routers, rack servers and modems can be mounted in a rack. **R** shows the front view with all ports; in Design you can re-plug there directly.
help.floors.title: Floors
help.floors.body: Large networks can be spread over floors. Cables between floors appear as risers.
help.snapshots.title: Snapshots
help.snapshots.body: A snapshot records a checkpoint. One is created automatically when the simulation starts and every five minutes while things change. Any snapshot can be restored in Design (undo with Ctrl+Z). Snapshots are saved with the project.

catalog.budgetOffice.description: A small office with four PCs needs a network. The customer will spend at most CHF 4,800 (the PCs are included). Pick a suitable switch in the shop and cable everything. «View → Costs» shows the bill.
catalog.budgetOffice.goal1: There is a switch in the network.

catalog.serverGroup.description: The client group stands for the 25 PCs of a classroom. Connect it to the switch and set up a DHCP service on the server with enough addresses for everyone.
catalog.serverGroup.goal1: The classroom is connected to the switch.
catalog.serverGroup.goal2: All 25 devices get an address via DHCP.

catalog.vlanColors.description: The switch ports are already split into VLAN 10 (office) and VLAN 20 (lab). Give both VLANs a name and a colour under «Tools → VLANs». The ports on the canvas are then coloured automatically.

catalog.vlanColors.goal2: VLAN 20 has a name and a colour.

catalog.stpLoop.description: Three switches are connected in a triangle so that one cable may fail. Without spanning tree, broadcasts circulate forever. Start the simulation and watch the broadcast storm. Fix it without removing a cable.
catalog.stpLoop.goal2: PC A reaches PC C by ping.
catalog.stpLoop.goal3: All three switches are still there (redundancy stays).

catalog.internetNat.description: The PC has a private address. To reach the web server on the Internet, the home router needs a default route to the provider and NAT on its WAN interface.

catalog.modemVdsl.description: Router and modem are set up; only the line to the provider is missing. Connect the VDSL modem with the right kind of line and watch in the packet list how it trains the line and logs in via PPPoE.

On R1 create “interface loopback0” with 10.255.0.1/32, on R2 10.255.0.2/32. Enable OSPF on both (all networks, area 0) and use the loopback address as router ID (“router-id 10.255.0.1”).
catalog.loopbackOspf.goal1: R1 knows R2's loopback (10.255.0.2/32) via OSPF.
catalog.loopbackOspf.hint1: Loopbacks are always up – OSPF announces them as /32.
catalog.aclGuest.title: Guest port with access list
catalog.aclGuest.description: A guest notebook is connected to the office switch (port 2). Guests may only use the portal on the web server (192.168.1.80, HTTP port 80) but must not reach other office devices. Create an access list GAST on the switch (“ip access-list extended GAST”, “permit tcp any host 192.168.1.80 eq 80”) and apply it to the guest port for incoming packets (“interface port2”, “ip access-group GAST in”). The list drops everything else by itself.
catalog.aclGuest.goal1: The guest notebook opens the web page on 192.168.1.80.
catalog.aclGuest.goal2: Blocked: the guest notebook does not reach PC Büro.
catalog.aclGuest.goal3: PC Büro still reaches the web server.
catalog.aclGuest.hint2: Every list ends with an invisible “deny ip any any”.
catalog.vrfCustomers.title: VRF: two customers with the same networks
catalog.vrfCustomers.description: A provider connects two sites (Basel and Geneva) for each of two customers. Both customers use the same networks 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.1.2.0/24. Customer A is already connected. On the router “PE Provider”, create the VRFs KUNDE-A and KUNDE-B (“vrf definition KUNDE-A”), assign the ports (“vrf forwarding KUNDE-A”: eth0 and eth1 for customer A, eth2 and eth3 for customer B) and give customer B's ports the addresses 10.1.1.1/24 and 10.1.2.1/24.
catalog.vrfCustomers.goal3: Question: why may both customers use the same networks?
catalog.vrfCustomers.hint2: The same addresses on one router only work if the ports are in different VRFs.
catalog.datacenter.title: Data centre: leaf-spine with BGP and VXLAN
catalog.datacenter.description: A data centre following the leaf-spine model: each leaf is connected to both spines, every link is its own /30 network (already addressed), every switch has a loopback 10.255.0.x/32. Set up the underlay with eBGP: spines AS 65000, leaf 1 to 3 AS 65001 to 65003; every switch announces its loopback (“network 10.255.0.11 mask 255.255.255.255”). Then the overlay: VXLAN with the loopback as source (“interface nve1”, “source-interface loopback0”), VNI 10010 for VLAN 10 (Web 1 and Web 2) and VNI 10020 for VLAN 20 (DB 1 and DB 2), with the other leafs' loopbacks as peers.
catalog.datacenter.goal1: Leaf 1 has two BGP sessions (to both spines).
catalog.datacenter.goal2: Leaf 1 knows Leaf 3's loopback (10.255.0.13/32) via BGP.
catalog.datacenter.goal5: Counter-check: Web 1 does not reach DB 1 (other VLAN, no gateway).
catalog.datacenter.hint3: The VTEPs must reach each other via their loopbacks – check the underlay first (“show ip route”, “show ip bgp summary”).
catalog.m145ue02.title: UE02 Old-school network: two networks with one router
catalog.m145ue02.description: The company still separates development and administration the “classic” way: each department has its own switch, the router connects the two networks. Router: port 1 (to the development switch) 192.168.1.1/24, port 2 (to the administration switch) 192.168.2.1/24. Development PCs 192.168.1.10 and .11, administration 192.168.2.10 and .11, gateway is the router.
catalog.m145ue02.goal1: Router has the address 192.168.1.1/24 in the development network.
catalog.m145ue02.goal2: Router has the address 192.168.2.1/24 in the administration network.
catalog.m145ue02.goal3: The PCs of each department reach each other (ping).
catalog.m145ue02.goal4: PC Entwicklung 1 uses the router as gateway (192.168.1.1).
catalog.m145ue02.goal5: PC Entwicklung 1 reaches PC Verwaltung 1 through the router.
catalog.m145ue02.hint5: Without a gateway the PC does not know where to send packets for another network.
catalog.m145ue03.title: UE03 Port-based VLAN: two departments on one switch
catalog.m145ue03.description: Instead of two switches there is only the switch on the 1st floor. Create VLAN 10 (ENTWICKLUNG) and VLAN 20 (VERWALTUNG) and assign the ports: development PCs to VLAN 10, administration PCs to VLAN 20. The PC addresses are already set (192.168.10.x and 192.168.20.x). Command line: “vlan 10”, “name ENTWICKLUNG”, “interface port1”, “switchport access vlan 10”.
catalog.m145ue03.goal6: Question: how many broadcast domains does the switch have now (not counting VLAN 1)?
catalog.m145ue03.hint1: A VLAN must be created first (“vlan 10”), otherwise the switch does not forward it.
catalog.m145ue04.title: UE04 Trunk VLAN: VLANs across two floors
catalog.m145ue04.description: A second switch is added on the 2nd floor, with two more VERWALTUNG PCs (VLAN 20), one SALES PC (VLAN 30, 192.168.30.0/24) and one ITMGMT PC (VLAN 40, 192.168.40.0/24). Create the VLANs on the 2nd floor, assign the ports and connect both switches with a trunk (port 8 on both sides, “switchport mode trunk”). Administration should form one network across both floors.
catalog.m145ue04.goal4: The link Switch 1OG – Switch 2OG is a trunk carrying VLAN 20.
catalog.m145ue04.goal5: Administration reaches each other across both floors (ping).
catalog.m145ue04.goal6: Counter-check: PC Verwaltung 3 does not reach PC Sales 1.
catalog.m145ue04.hint4: Both ends must be trunks, and the VLAN must exist on both switches.
catalog.m145ue05.title: UE05 VLAN theory check: who receives the broadcast?
catalog.m145ue05.description: Four switches form a chain. Look closely at the ports (“Ports” window or “show interfaces trunk”): between Switch B and Switch C there are two access ports, between Switch C and Switch D a trunk. First work out step by step on the worksheet which PCs receive a broadcast from PC A (VLAN 10). Then check in the simulation: open the packet list and ping an unknown address in the network from PC A (e.g. 192.168.99.99) – who gets the ARP request?
catalog.m145ue05.goal1: Which PCs receive a broadcast from PC A?
catalog.m145ue05.goal2: Which trunk setting between Switch C and Switch D differs on the two sides?
catalog.m145ue05.goal3: PC A reaches PC G by ping (although the path goes through VLAN 20).
catalog.m145ue05.hint1: Untagged frames end up in the VLAN of the receiving port (access VLAN or native VLAN).
catalog.m145ue06.title: UE06 Router on a stick: routing between VLANs
catalog.m145ue06.description: For the VLANs to talk to each other you need a router (inter-VLAN routing). Connect “Router 1OG” (port 1) to port 7 of Switch 1OG and make that port a trunk. Create one subinterface per VLAN on the router (eth0.10 to eth0.40, “encapsulation dot1q 10”, address 192.168.<VLAN>.1/24). All four VLANs must exist on both switches, and all PCs need their gateway .1.
catalog.m145ue06.goal2: Switch 1OG – Router 1OG: trunk with VLAN 10, 20, 30 and 40 (subinterfaces on the router).
catalog.m145ue06.goal3: Switch 1OG – Switch 2OG: trunk with VLAN 20, 30 and 40.
catalog.m145ue06.goal5: All departments reach each other: ENTWICKLUNG, VERWALTUNG, SALES and ITMGMT (ping).
catalog.m145ue06.hint3: Switch 1OG lacks VLAN 30 and 40 at the start.
catalog.m145ue06.hint5: Tagging on the router: “encapsulation dot1q <VLAN>” on the subinterface.
catalog.m145ue07.title: UE07 Layer 3 switch: routing with SVIs
catalog.m145ue07.description: A layer 3 switch replaces the router and switch on the 1st floor. VLANs, ports and the trunk to the 2nd floor are already set up, the PCs have their gateway .1. Create one VLAN interface (SVI) per VLAN on the L3 switch: “interface vlan 10”, “ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0” and so on for VLAN 20, 30 and 40. Routing must be switched on.
catalog.m145ue07.goal1: PC Entwicklung 1 reaches its gateway on the L3 switch.
catalog.m145ue07.goal3: Question: which command switches on routing on the L3 switch (in configuration mode)?
catalog.m145ue07b.title: UE07b Layer 3 switch with ACL
catalog.m145ue07b.description: After inter-VLAN routing all VLANs can talk to each other. Now traffic is controlled with access lists (ACL) on the VLAN interfaces: ITMGMT may use ICMP (ping) into all VLANs. ENTWICKLUNG is isolated except for access from ITMGMT. VERWALTUNG and SALES may talk to each other. Everything else is blocked – only what is needed is allowed (no “permit ip any any”). Command line: “ip access-list extended VLAN10-IN”, “permit icmp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255”, “interface vlan 10”, “ip access-group VLAN10-IN in”.
catalog.m145ue07b.goal1: ITMGMT reaches ENTWICKLUNG, VERWALTUNG and SALES by ping.
catalog.m145ue07b.goal2: VERWALTUNG and SALES reach each other (both floors).
catalog.m145ue07b.goal3: Blocked: VERWALTUNG does not reach ENTWICKLUNG.
catalog.m145ue07b.goal4: Blocked: SALES does not reach ENTWICKLUNG.
catalog.m145ue07b.goal5: Blocked: ENTWICKLUNG does not reach SALES.
catalog.m145ue07b.hint1: A ping needs both directions: the reply (echo reply) passes the list of the other VLAN.
catalog.m145ue07b.hint3: “show access-lists” shows which rule matches how often.
catalog.m145ue08.title: UE08 DHCP on the layer 3 switch
catalog.m145ue08.description: So far all addresses are static. On the L3 switch, create a DHCP pool per VLAN (“ip dhcp pool VLAN10”, “network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0”, “default-router 192.168.10.1”, “dns-server 198.51.100.53”) and exclude the addresses .1 to .9 (“ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.9”). Then switch the PCs to DHCP. The DNS server is the public server 198.51.100.53 (example address).
catalog.m145ue08.goal1: PC Entwicklung 1 gets its address by DHCP, with DNS server {dns}.
catalog.m145ue08.goal2: PC Verwaltung 3 (2nd floor) gets its address by DHCP, with DNS server {dns}.
catalog.m145ue08.goal3: PC Sales 1 gets its address by DHCP.
catalog.m145ue08.goal4: PC ITMGMT 1 gets its address by DHCP.
catalog.m145ue08.goal5: PC Entwicklung 2 reaches PC Sales 1 (both with DHCP address).
catalog.m145ue08.hint1: Are the PCs switched to DHCP?
catalog.m145ue09.title: UE09 External DHCP: central server with relay
catalog.m145ue09.description: Instead of the L3 switch, a central DHCP server in administration (1st floor) now hands out addresses. Connect the server to port 5 of the L3 switch in VLAN 20 and give it 192.168.20.200/24 (gateway .1). On the server set up the range for its own network (192.168.20.100 to .199) and under “Additional scopes” one range .100 to .199 for each of VLAN 10, 30 and 40, each with gateway .1. On the L3 switch enter the server as DHCP relay on VLAN interfaces 10, 30 and 40 (“ip helper-address 192.168.20.200”) and remove the pools on the switch (“no ip dhcp pool VLAN10” etc.).
catalog.m145ue09.goal2: The server hands out 192.168.20.100 to .199 in VLAN 20 with gateway 192.168.20.1.
catalog.m145ue09.goal3: PC Verwaltung 1 gets its address by DHCP.
catalog.m145ue09.goal4: PC Sales 1 gets 192.168.30.100 from the central server via the relay.
catalog.m145ue09.goal5: PC ITMGMT 1 gets 192.168.40.100 from the central server via the relay.
catalog.m145ue09.goal6: PC Entwicklung 1 reaches the DHCP server.
catalog.m145ue09.hint4: The server picks the range whose network contains the relay address (giaddr).
catalog.m145ue10.title: UE10 Network design: three-tier (core, distribution, access)
catalog.m145ue10.description: A campus following the three-layer model: Core 1 and Core 2 (routers) are addressed and connect to the server, the access layer is done (one VLAN per floor, trunk to distribution). Set up the distribution layer: Distribution 1 serves VLAN 10 and 20, Distribution 2 VLAN 30 and 40 – create VLANs, ports to the access switches as trunks, one gateway per VLAN (SVI 192.168.<VLAN>.1/24). A transfer network leads to the core: Distribution 1 port 1 in VLAN 901 with SVI 10.255.1.2/30, Distribution 2 port 1 in VLAN 902 with SVI 10.255.2.2/30. Finally OSPF (area 0) on all four routers and L3 switches.
catalog.m145ue10.goal1: PC Etage 1 reaches PC Etage 2 (routing in Distribution 1).
catalog.m145ue10.goal2: Core 1 has at least two OSPF neighbours (Core 2, Distribution 1).
catalog.m145ue10.goal4: Through the core: floor 1 – floor 4, floor 3 – server, floor 2 – floor 3 (ping).
catalog.m145ue10.goal5: Question: which layer routes between the floor VLANs here?
catalog.m145ue10.hint2: OSPF for all networks: “router ospf 1”, “network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0”.
catalog.m145ue11.title: UE11 Network design: collapsed core
catalog.m145ue11.description: An SME network in the two-layer model: core switches A and B take over core and distribution. Each access switch is connected redundantly to both (port 7 to Core A, port 8 to Core B), Core A and Core B are linked via port 1. That creates loops: switch on spanning tree on all switches and make Core A the root bridge (priority 4096). VLANs: office 1 = 10, office 2 = 20, office 3 = 30, server = 100 (Core A port 5). All links between switches are trunks. Core A is the gateway for all VLANs (SVI 192.168.<VLAN>.1/24).
catalog.m145ue11.goal1: No broadcast storm despite redundant cables.
catalog.m145ue11.goal2: Access 1 – Core B is a trunk with VLAN 10 (backup path).
catalog.m145ue11.goal3: Office 1 reaches office 3, office 2 reaches the server (ping).
catalog.m145ue11.goal5: Question: which layers does the collapsed core combine?
catalog.m145ue11.hint1: Without spanning tree, broadcasts circle endlessly over the redundant paths.
catalog.m145x1.title: Extra 1: troubleshooting router on a stick
catalog.m145x1.description: The network from UE06 no longer works: four faults are hidden (switches, trunk, router, PCs). Find and fix them without rebuilding the network. Helpful: “show vlan brief”, “show interfaces trunk”, “show ip interface brief”, “ipconfig” and the packet list.
catalog.m145x1.hint1: Does VLAN 30 exist on both switches, and does the trunk allow it?
catalog.m145x1.hint2: Is the tag on the VLAN 40 subinterface correct?
catalog.m145x2.title: Extra 2: management VLAN and native VLAN
catalog.m145x2.description: The switches should be reachable from ITMGMT through their own management VLAN. Create VLAN 99 (MGMT) and VLAN 999 (NATIVE) on both switches. Switch 2OG gets “interface vlan 99” with 192.168.99.12/24 and default gateway 192.168.99.1 (“ip default-gateway”), the L3 switch an SVI 192.168.99.1/24. On the trunk between the floors set the native VLAN to 999 on both sides (“switchport trunk native vlan 999”).
catalog.m145x2.goal1: The trunk L3-Switch 1OG – Switch 2OG carries VLAN 99.
catalog.m145x2.goal2: PC ITMGMT 1 reaches the management address of Switch 2OG.
catalog.m145x2.goal3: Everything else keeps working: PC ITMGMT 1 reaches PC Verwaltung 1.
catalog.m145x2.goal4: Question: why set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN?
catalog.m145x3.title: Extra 3: port channel between the floors
catalog.m145x3.description: There is a second cable between the L3 switch and Switch 2OG (port 7 on both sides), both ports are trunks – without bundling, broadcasts circle. Combine port 7 and port 8 on both switches into a port channel with LACP (“interface range port7 - 8”, “channel-group 1 mode active”). Then both cables share the load, and if one fails, traffic continues over the other.
catalog.m145x3.goal2: The link between the floors is a trunk with VLAN 20, 30 and 40.
catalog.m145x3.goal3: Administration across both floors and development to ITMGMT (ping).

catalog.vpnSites.title: VPN: connecting Zürich and Bern
catalog.vpnSites.description: Both sites are reachable via the Internet, but their private networks are not: the Internet does not forward private addresses. Connect the networks with an IPsec tunnel between the routers.
catalog.vpnSites.hint1: Router Zürich → Advanced → VPN: peer 203.0.113.1, local network 192.168.1.0/24, remote network 192.168.2.0/24, a key of your choice.
catalog.vpnSites.hint2: Enter the same tunnel mirrored on router Bern: peer 198.51.100.1, networks swapped, same key.
catalog.bgpTwoAs.title: Two autonomous systems with BGP
catalog.bgpTwoAs.description: The company (AS 65001) and its provider (AS 65002) exchange their networks via BGP. Configure BGP on both routers, add the neighbour and announce your own network.
catalog.bgpTwoAs.goal1: The BGP session between the routers is established.
catalog.bgpTwoAs.hint1: R Firma: AS 65001, neighbour 172.16.12.2 with AS 65002. R Provider the other way round.
catalog.bgpTwoAs.hint2: Without announced networks the session is up but no routes arrive.
catalog.portShutdown.title: Lock out the guest
catalog.portShutdown.description: A foreign notebook is plugged into the switch. Shut down its switch port without removing the cable. This also works during simulation: turn the port off in the switch's port table.
catalog.portShutdown.goal1: PC 1 can no longer reach the guest.
catalog.portShutdown.hint1: Click the switch and turn off the port to the guest in the port table (shutdown).
catalog.vlsm.title: Subnets by need (VLSM)
catalog.vlsm.description: Split 192.168.10.0/24 so that Office can connect 100, Lab 50 and Guests 20 devices without wasting addresses. The IP calculator (key I) helps: «By host count», then «Apply». The router gets the first address of each subnet.
catalog.vlsm.goal4: Office reaches Guests through the router.
catalog.vlsm.hint1: Largest network first: 100 hosts need 7 bits → /25.
catalog.vlsm.hint4: Each PC needs its subnet's router address as gateway.
catalog.fiberOnt.title: Fibre connection
catalog.fiberOnt.description: Router and ONT (fibre modem) are set up. Connect the ONT to the provider with fibre and watch in the packet list how it registers via PLOAM and OMCI.
catalog.fiberOnt.goal1: The ONT is connected to the provider by fibre.
catalog.fiberOnt.goal3: The PC reaches the server on the Internet.
catalog.fiberOnt.hint1: In the shop under «Connections» pick the fibre cable, then click the ONT and the provider.
catalog.ripChain.title: RIP in a chain
catalog.ripChain.description: Three routers in a row but no routes. Enable RIP on all three and add their networks. Watch the RIP responses in the packet list and the «R» entries in the routing table.
catalog.ripChain.goal1: R1 knows PC 3's network via RIP.
catalog.ripChain.hint1: Click a router → routing protocols → enable RIP → «Add own networks».

about.story1: Mark teaches networking. For years he and his classes pulled cables in Cisco Packet Tracer and FILIUS, sent pings and conjured up broadcast storms (mostly on purpose). At some point it was clear: there has to be a tool that is more modern, does more, simply runs in the browser and can still be installed locally.
about.story2: So Mark knocked on his brother Mika's door. Together they put up the scaffolding. Then Mark took the wheel and added idea after idea from the classroom, from colourful VLANs to BGP.
about.story3: To be honest: without artificial intelligence there would be no leyoNET. The actual programming is done by an AI. The ideas, the classroom experience, the decisions and the responsibility when a packet goes missing lie with Mark and Mika.
about.story4: And the name? «leyo» are the initials of Mark's children. The symbol shows an «l» and a «y» made of network nodes: «ly» for «love you». After all, every good network needs strong connections.
